utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will the Registrar call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-04-82-A, the Prosecutor versus Ljube Boskoski and Johan Tarculovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Boskoski, I'm to ask you whether can you hear me and follow the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOSKOSKI
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And Mr. Tarculovski, can you hear me and follow the proceedings through the translation. THE ACCUSED TARCULOVSKI: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we have the appearances, beginning with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Mr. President. Your Honours, Paul Rogers appearing on behalf of the Prosecution today, together with Ms. Laurel Baig, Mr. Francois Boudreault, and Ms. Nadia Shihata. Your Honours, they will be dealing with the Tarculovski part of the appeal. This afternoon I will be joined by Ms. Elena Martin-Salgado and two of my colleagues will leave, so there will be a change of personnel whilst I deal with the Boskoski part of the appeal. So you know what will happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have an abundance of resources, Mr. Rogers. You're blessed. And then for Mr. Boskoski.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. For Mr. Boskoski, Edina Residovic, Guenael Mettraux and our assistants will be representing Mr. Boskoski this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And for Mr. Tarculovski. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: May it please the Court, Mr. President, Mr. Alan Dershowitz for the appellant Mr. Tarculovski, and my brother Nathan Dershowitz. We will dividing the argument. I will be doing the first 30 minutes; he will be doing the second 45 minutes. And with the permission of the Court, if there is any time that we do not use in our opening argument, we would like to add that to our time for our rebuttal argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we'll consider that, Mr. Dershowitz. Let me summarise the appeals. The appeals concern the events during and subsequent to a police operation conducted on the 12th of August, 2001, in the village of Ljuboten, situated in the northern part of the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia. Johan Tarculovski and the Prosecution appeal from a Judgement rendered on the 10th of July, 2008, by Trial Chamber II. The Chamber found Johan Tarculovski guilty of charges of ordering, planning, and instigating murder as a violation of the laws or customs of war; wanton destruction as a violation of the laws or customs of war, Count 2; and cruel treatment as a violation of the laws or customs of war, Count 3. The Trial Chamber sentenced Johan Tarculovski to a single sentence of imprisonment of 12 years. Ljube Boskoski was found not guilty of all charges and the Prosecution appeals his acquittal. Johan Tarculovski initially filed his notice of appeal on the 8th of August, 2008, setting out 15 grounds. On the 12th of January, he filed his appeal brief, setting out seven grounds of appeal. With the leave of the Appeals Chamber, on the 2nd of April, 2009, Tarculovski filed his amended notice of appeal, corresponding to his appeal brief. The Prosecution filed its response brief on the 9th of April, 2009. Tarculovski filed his reply brief on the 24th of April, 2009. The Prosecution filed its notice of appeal on the 6th of August, 2008, and its appeal brief on the 20th of October, 2008. Ljube Boskoski filed his response brief on the 1st of December, 2008, and the Prosecution filed its reply brief on the 16th of December. I will now summarise the grounds of appeal. Johan Tarculovski brings seven grounds of appeal and seeks an acquittal on all counts. On the first ground of appeal he submits that the Tribunal's exercise of jurisdiction over this matter is improper. Since the Tribunal did not make a threshold determination as to whether the government of the FYROM lawfully ordered the operation in self-defence to root out terrorists from amongst the villagers. Under his second ground of appeal, he submits that the events in Ljuboten on the 12th of August, 2001, did not violate the laws or customs of war since they were the result of a sovereign's legitimate and proportionate response to an internal terrorist attack. He also questions the applicability of the laws or customs of war in determining individual criminal responsibility for a person assigned to carry out a legitimate operation planned by a sovereign. In his third ground of appeal, he submits that the Trial Chamber erred in its application of Article 7(1) of the Statute with respect to planning, instigating, or ordering. In Ground 4, he alleges that the evidence was insufficient to find the murder, wanton destruction, and cruel treatment as established beyond a reasonable doubt. In his fifth ground, he argues that the Trial Chamber improperly rejected the testimony of entire categories of witnesses, while it later selectively relied upon the supposedly rejected testimony. His sixth ground of appeal concerns his statements to a commission established by the Ministry of Interior to investigate what had occurred in Ljuboten. Tarculovski argues that these statements were improperly admitted or, alternatively, improperly used. And in his last ground of appeal, he requests the Appeals Chamber to reduce his sentence. The Prosecution brings one ground of appeal, in relation to the acquittal of Ljube Boskoski. It argues that the Trial Chamber erred in law in finding that Boskoski had taken the necessary and reasonable measures to punish, under Article 7(3) of the Statute, since the Trial Chamber applied the wrong legal standard. Alternatively, it argues that the Trial Chamber erred in fact since Boskoski failed to take certain measures that were necessary and reasonable to punish his offending subordinates. The Prosecution argues that it was possible, necessary and reasonable for Boskoski to inquire into the facts of the crimes, report the alleged criminal conduct of his subordinates to the competent authorities, and initiate disciplinary proceedings against these subordinates. I bring to the attention of the parties that by a letter of the 20th of October, the Chamber invited the parties to address a specific issue during this hearing. There is no need for me to restate that issue at this time. The hearing will proceed according to the Scheduling Order issued on the 2nd of September, 2009. Counsel for Johan Tarculovski will present his submissions this morning for 1 hour and 15 minutes. They have indicated a division of that time. Following a 30-minute pause, the Prosecution will present its response for one hour; following which counsel for Johan Tarculovski will reply for 20 minutes. There will then be a break for one hour. The hearing will continue in the afternoon with the appeal of the Prosecution for 1 hour and 15 minutes, and a response from counsel for Ljube Boskoski for one hour, and the Prosecution's reply for 20 minutes. The parties are reminded to present their submissions in a precise and clear manner. Madam Registrar, you will assist with the time keeping. I now invite counsel for Mr. Tarculovski to present his submissions, Mr. Alan Dershowitz. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: Mr. President, and may it please the Tribunal, my name is Alan Dershowitz, and I'm here on behalf of Johan Tarculovski. The issue in this appeal -- still not -- is this better?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's on, yes. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: If I stand straight you won't hear? It's okay now? Okay. Thank you. The issue on this appeal is presented very squarely by the parties. The Prosecution argues throughout its brief that "the question of whether the Ljuboten operation was in self-defence against terrorists is 'irrelevant.'" That's their position throughout the brief. We argue that this question was central, if not dispositive, both on the issues of jurisdiction and on the issues of culpability. There is, in our view, a dispositive difference between an operation that has no legitimate military purpose, such as genocide, ethnic cleansing, wanton destruction of property, murder of civilians, and a legitimate military operation that produced some civilian deaths in the process of defending against terrorism. Acts of terrorism have become almost routine around the world, terrorists occur -- acts occur within countries, across borders, even across oceans and continents. States that are victimised by terrorist activities often respond, claiming that they are targeting only terrorists. States that harbour terrorists often claim that the targets were civilians. Whether a victim was a terrorist or a civilian is often a matter of degree. This is an continuum of civilianality that has been recognised in the literature. An individual may engage in a terrorist act and then return to civilian status. A village may actively support and hide terrorists, or the villagers may be victims themselves, forced to harbour or become human shields for terrorists. Each situation presents different concerns and the applicable rules that govern these concerns are being hotly debated in the academy today. The Prosecution conceded that the defendant in this case was ordered to conduct a search of the village of Ljuboten for a man named Xhavit Hasani, and that he acted on that order. The Trial Tribunal itself found: "There is some evidence which could suggest that a number of Ljuboten residents were involved in the planting of the land-mine on 10 August, resulting in the death of eight Macedonian soldiers. And it also found that for this reason the Chamber accepts that on the basis of the information available to the police, there were legitimate reasons for the police to enter the village of Ljuboten on August 12th because of a suspected terrorist or NLA presence." There is far different legally from a situation where there was no legitimate military reason for undertaking the operation. The laws and customs of war are clear in the latter situation, but they are utterly, utterly unclear when military action is taken against terrorists who hide among civilians and who do not wear military uniforms. The Prosecution argued in this case that the government of Macedonia had no right to go into Ljuboten on August 12th, 2001, that it did not matter whether the government honestly and reasonably believed that the NLA was in Ljuboten, and aimed the operation at the NLA. According to the Prosecution, any military action on that day was inappropriate because the NLA's killing of ten soldiers on August 8th and eight soldiers near Ljuboten on August 10th had created "an incendiary climate." Your Honours, think of the implications of that argument. If adopted, it would never be appropriate for a sovereign to respond to domestic terrorism because terrorist acts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Dershowitz, I'm told that the French interpreter is asking you to speak more slowly. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: I appreciate that. Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you. I'm sorry for speaking quickly. The Prosecution's argument is that any time there is an act of terrorism, essentially it will always create a volatile situation. In effect, the Prosecution is arguing that the greater the need for intervention and self-defence, the less the right to do so. This principle has never been accepted as fundamental international law. Moreover, as the Tribunal is fully aware, Article 51 of the Charter of the United Nations precludes second guessing, essentially, of sovereign military decisions based on reasonable fear and reasonable acts of self-defence. If a member state may even engage in pre-emptive actions across borders, a fortiori, a member state may act in reaction and in self-defence within its own territories. This Tribunal, the trial Tribunal never resolved this issue in any meaningful way. The Prosecution argument does not accept, does not represent accepted international legal norms. Scholars, for example, such as Professor Michael Schmitt, the dean and professor of international law at the George Marshall European Center for Security Services and currently a visiting professor at the Naval College in the United States, have concluded that this complex issue, the complex issue of what right a sovereign has when terrorists are hiding among civilians, is a subject "unaddressed in lex scripta," and there is no treaty norm addressing this issue. It is not surprising therefore that neither the Prosecution, nor the Trial Tribunal, have cited a single authority, any law or even any consensus scholarship on this issue. The Tribunal has jurisdiction to prosecute only "persons violating the laws or customs of war." And we submit that there are no laws or customs currently governing the conduct at issue in this case. The military, in rooting out terrorists from among civilian shields, presents a dilemma that is ongoing in the academic literature and in the professional and juridical literature. There are, of course, rules of proportionality. Even those rules are extraordinarily complex when it comes to terrorist activities, as evidenced by what is ongoing today in Iraq and Afghanistan, and Gaza, and a range of other places around the world. There is not even consensus on how the rule of proportionality operates. Indeed we cite in our brief several scholars that point to three different rules of proportionality that can operate this context. But the defendant here, importantly, was not charged with violating rules of proportionality; that's not the way the Prosecution presented the case. And the reason they didn't present the case that way is, obviously when three people are killed in a military attack or three non-terrorists in a military attack, responding to the killing of 18 people previously, they would be hard-pressed to make any claim of proportionality. He was instead charged with planning, inciting, murder, destruction of property and cruel treatment of non-combatants on the basis of what we submit is a circular and impermissible inference in a terror shield situation. Namely, that -- here I'm quoting from the trial Tribunal as they put it: "What was done -- what was done by a group of police in the village in the presence of the leader of the group," and we dispute that characterisation, "what was done provides a significant and reliable guide to what was intended as the object of the operation." And then using that circular improper inference, and I'll explain in a minute why it is improper, they come to the following conclusion. An object, not the object, an object - this is important now, apparently, apparently, and I underline that word, apparently the predominant object was to indiscriminately attack civilians. In the first place, Your Honours, "apparently" is not beyond a reasonable doubt. "Apparently" is an admission of speculation, inference, and lack of absolute evidence in this case. And my brother will document, point by point, the lack of evidence on this point. But reasoning from result to intent, the old British notion of man intends the natural consequences of his conduct, has been rejected. The United States Supreme Court, for example, in a leading case called Sandstrom v. Montana, said under American constitutional law it would be unconstitutional to infer intent from result. It is always a questionable inference. But it is particularly irrational and false in a situation like this one. Where A, the Prosecution and the Tribunal concede that the original purpose was to root out terrorists. Nobody has presented any evidence to the contrary about the crucial meeting on the eve of the operation; B, the Tribunal found that "there were legitimate reasons to enter the village and that there may well have been terrorists living among the civilians"; C, three of the deaths were of NLA terrorists, and medical help was administered to some of the wounded; D, the Tribunal "accepts that it may have been believed by army personnel that there was" - and this is crucial - "ongoing fire directed at the police during the operation." That is a finding of the Tribunal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Dershowitz. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I make you back to the word "apparently." If the Tribunal had found not apparently but certainly and beyond a reasonable doubt that the predominant object was to indiscriminately attack civilians, would that make any difference your argument? MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: Your Honour, it would very much depend on a range of issues that I'm going to be talking about now; that is, the nature of the operation, whether -- we wouldn't waive our jurisdictional arguments but assuming that there was subject matter jurisdiction, the Court has already found that there was geographical and temporal jurisdiction, but assuming there was jurisdiction that covered the subject matter, if there were proof, specific proof, I'm not talking about finding now because a finding be questioned, obviously, in front of the Tribunal. But if there were proof, if there a tape-recording, for example, of the meeting, let's give you an example. The Wannsee Conference that occurred in Germany in the 1940s, there were documents about what occurred. There was a meeting in Wannsee. They decided at that meeting that they were going to simply systematically round up and kill Jews. Or if there were of a videotape of a meeting, say, dealing with Srebrenica and there were -- was evidence and clear proof that there was no military, no military operation at all, that this was purely designed as ethnic cleansing, yes, the case would be considerably different. What we're arguing is, when you have at worse a mixed case, a case where there is no evidence of anything other than a plan to root out terrorists in the beginning -- and remember, too, the government in this case understands how weak its position is and it actually presents a fallback position to the Court, where it says that the Prosecution -- I'm not quoting yet. The Prosecution concedes that the plan "may not have been in place before the police entered the village but may have developed after the first crimes were committed." Think of that, Your Honours what that means. What they're conceding is that there was no plan in the beginning. The plan in the beginning may have been perfectly legitimate and perfectly military, and then in the fog of war, after the first crimes were committed, suddenly, a plan developed? And my defendant, without any evidence, is regarded as having developed the plan and implemented the plan? It's a complete change of theory and a major acknowledgment, we believe, of the weakness of their case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Judge Meron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Very interesting argument, Mr. Dershowitz. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: It strikes me that your a fortiori invocation of Article 51 to internal conflicts is -- might be a bit thin. Is -- are you arguing that this was a law enforcement action or a war-like operation? MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: Well, we think it was more -- certainly it was mixed in some ways. It was mixed. It involved police. Today, of course, in the war against terrorism, police often have armoured vehicles. They often have helicopters. The distinction between a police action and a military action is often a matter of degree. We think this is closer to a police action than a military action. But obviously it had elements of both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: If it was a police action, then the normal restraints applicable to police operation in terms of targeting would be perhaps more rigorous than those that would apply to a war-like situation. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: Well, there is a great debate, as Your Honour is aware, of whether or not terrorism is law enforcement issue or is a military issue. There is no singular answer to that question. And our basic point is, Your Honour, these complex issues ought not to be revolved on the back of a 26-year-old inexperienced man who knew nothing about international law. We are here debating this issue and he is in jail, in prison, because he guessed wrong, as the Court said, between right and wrong in the fog of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: But what parameters would you suggest to sort of reassure against a complete laissez-faire for the -- for armies or police forces in those cases? If your argument regarding self-defence against terrorism to which, as you argue, very few rules are applicable, can this not be abused? MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Is not the claim of terrorism made everywhere? I mean, in Sudan, everywhere, you have that claim and the international judges are confronted with a need to have some rational criteria. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: Absolutely, Your Honour. I agree completely. And first of all, the finding -- this Tribunal already made a finding that there was terrorism and that there was a legitimate interest in going in and attacking and rooting out terrorism. So we're not presented with the Sudan issue in this case. Second, the rules of proportionality. Those are the rules that, it seems to me, have to govern this kind of situation. And there is a complicated issue in this case, Your Honour, which I'm sure you are aware of. There is a rule that says when in doubt, you should assume that somebody is a civilian rather than a non-combatant. But then the rules of beyond a reasonable require Tribunals to take the opposite assumption; that is, although the person on the ground should always err on the side of assuming somebody is a civilian, the Court must always err on the side of assuming that the defendant was not aware that the person was a civilian. So, as Your Honour may or may not know, and here I have to get a little personal, I have written a book on this subject called "Preemption," in which I call for a new jurisprudence to deal and regulate these issues. And I'm not alone in calling for a new jurisprudence. Virtually the entire academy recognises that the rules are unclear. I'm very sympathetic to the position of an international court that is anxious to apply rules of law, but they can't apply them retroactively. And it's not function of this court to create new rules and -- or the Tribunal, trial Tribunal, and apply them to a defendant in the fog of war. It would be perfectly reasonable for this Tribunal to lay out what it believes the problems are and the complexities and to acknowledge that the defendant in this case could not possibly have been aware are of what his duties were in -- when he is ordered by the president, the Court acknowledges, the Tribunal acknowledges this was not his idea. This was not his plan. He didn't carry it out in person. He didn't kill anybody. He is in this kind of intermediate position, not planner, not the killer, but the person it is claimed who was in charge, who led the operation; we dispute that. But nonetheless, even if that were true, what his obligations are beyond proportionality, even proportionality you would think that is an upper level decision, that is, the people deciding whether to go into this town or not would be responsible for the issue of proportionality. These are complex issues and I think for us to prevail in this appeal, with due respect, Your Honour, all we have to do is persuade the Court that the law is unclear. And that international humanitarian law and the law of war provide no clear guide-lines, no clear criteria for when it is appropriate to take actions that inevitably will result in the death of some civilians. Here look at the result. Three terrorists are killed. Three alleged non-terrorists, all male, all allegedly wearing black, were also killed. Under rules of proportionality that would not be seen to be impermissible. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Judge Liu, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to seek some clarifications concerning of the Ground 1 of your appeal. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: According to the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, whether attack was ordered as pre-emptive, defensive or even offensive is irrelevant in the point of -- in -- from the legal point of view and the question is whether the accused has committed some unlawful crimes during those military operations. Is it that your position that so long as the military action is lawful, just, or legitimate, this Tribunal will have no jurisdictions over whatever happened during that actions? MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: No, that's not our position, Your Honour. We concede, of course, that this Tribunal would have jurisdiction. Say, for example, that the Srebrenica events started out as legitimate attempts to stop terrorism, and then suddenly the decision was made to murder 7.000 individuals. The people who were responsible for making that decision, the people who implemented that decision would be responsible. What we're saying though is that in a case like this, where you have a relatively small number of people killed, proportional number of people killed, a relatively small amount of property destruction compared to the size of the village and what was going on previously, that it is certainly relevant, it is certainly relevant that the operation was legitimate. It is one of the major factors that have to be taken into consideration that the laws are different for genocidal operations, that started out as genocidal, that had no military function, and for operations that started out as legitimate and something may have happened in the process. Particularly for the person in the middle. Particularly for the person who didn't order the operation and the person who didn't carry out the operation but for the person who is held in this kind of middle category of responsibility. So the quote that Your Honour pointed to is a quote, of course, that talks about the relevance of preemption, the relevance of a range of other factors. We think that that quote is dictum and it also doesn't apply particularly in the context of this case. It would be revolutionary, Your Honour, revolutionary to the law of war to say that it makes no difference at all, that it is irrelevant whether an operation was lawful or whether an operation was unlawful. It certainly goes to the mens rea of the defendant. If a 26-year-old defendant is told to engage in a proper operation which then gets out of hand, obviously it's a different situation than if a 27-year-old person is told, Go and kill civilians. Now, in this case, Your Honour, it's obvious, if you look at the results, the results of a relatively small number of people killed, people sent to the hospital for their injuries, that's not what you do when you're engaged in a massive genocide. A range of other factors that certainly though -- that this was, at worst, a military-police action in which some policemen - we haven't been able to identify the policemen - may have engaged in crime, and the issue is the absence of evidence in this context that our defendant incited, ordered or in any other way was directly responsible. So, no, it would not end the discussion were this to be found to be a lawful military operation, but it does end the possibility of prosecution if the Tribunal found it without relevance at all, as the Prosecution argues. And remember the Prosecution also argues that it was impermissible to have a military operation on that day in that town. That was the essence or an essence of what they argued and we think that is it clearly not acceptable -- not an acceptable position under international law. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Mr. Dershowitz, you know that since the Tadic case in 1995, this Tribunal consistently held that there are rules which are applicable, rules of international law which are applicable also to internal conflict. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: And I would suggest that instead of focussing so much on justification ver nom [phoen], from which we normally steer away, you would try to explain to the Court why technically the rules of war were or were not observed. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Because this is our interest, rather than -- we usually are not persuaded by the arguments that the some operation was -- a military was or was not justified. For many years now, international humanitarian law insisted that whether a military operation is or is not justified, the rules of war applicable in military conflict must be observed. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: We agree, Your Honour. We certainly agree. We understand the distinction between the rules that permit an attack and the rules that govern once an attack occurs. Even if the Tribunal were to accept all of the arguments made by the Prosecution and all of the facts found by the Tribunal - and this is responding to your question, Judge Meron - the logic would lead exactly in the other direction. Let's assume that -- that you could look at intention and -- and discern intention from the result in a case, and this is why we think the rules of law were -- war were not violated. Here you have a situation - and my brother will go into this in even greater detail - where you are a planning meeting. We start out with a planning meeting. In the planning meeting all the evidence is that the plan was perfectly legitimate. Then the event is postponed for a day. Why? Because they have to do reconnaissance. You don't do reconnaissance for genocide. You do reconnaissance because you want to find out which houses and which people are terrorists and where the terrorists are hiding. Then you look at the result. The result, three dead out of thousands. All of the three suspected of being NLA terrorists. Maybe wrongly. Maybe wrongly. That is possible. Then you find medical assistance given to some of the wounded. If the purpose was to randomly kill civilians, many, many more would have had died. Many more women and children would have died. I know of no situation in the international jurisprudence where we found a war crime based on the incredible paucity of the numbers that were killed here, and that -- putting aside the fact that there is great dispute about whether this whole event, the Macedonian conflict with the NLA, is even an armed conflict with intensity, et cetera, et cetera. The Court, by the way, the Tribunal had grave doubts about that. It came to conclusions that suggest real, real concerns about whether or not there were these doubts. The Chamber takes into account that despite the clear escalation there remain relatively few casualties, on both sides, to civilians. The highest estimate put to the number of these killed during 2001 as a result of armed clashes is 168, and then it goes through the small number. Material damage to property and housing, relatively small scale. We know that the issue of event here itself -- what we're arguing, Your Honour, is, this is a case without evidence. This is a case without direct evidence of any war crime. What we have direct evidence is only results. Reasoning back from the results, we believe that you cannot come to the conclusion that war crimes occurred here. Now, without diminishing the death of three possibly innocent civilian men, the partial destruction of houses and the mistreatment of some other men. This is not the kind of war crime nor was this the kind of sustained intense armed conflict that is appropriately the subject of this court's jurisdiction. If you look, Your Honour, at the numbers here, they are certainly smaller than the numbers in Northern Ireland. And the panel conceded, and I think the Prosecution conceded, that the Northern Ireland conflict was not -- would not have been within the jurisdiction of international law. Nobody claimed that it was the kind of armed conflict that is governed by international law. This is closer to that, and the event in question is one of the smallest events. And so the idea of exercising jurisdiction in a relatively small case, in a relatively small conflict, has incredibly dangerous consequences for international law and for the jurisdiction of this Tribunal. The message that this case sends, and it is an absolutely false message, would be that this young, inexperienced man was the single worst offender in the Macedonian conflict. He is the only man who is in prison as the result of the Macedonian conflict, and his actions were somehow akin to others who are the appropriate subject of international law. Also, Your Honour, the ultimate object of this Tribunal, and this entire Tribunal is to promote peace. And we can represent to this Court that recently the representatives of the Albanian side, the representatives of the victim side, would not be opposed to an end of the situation. The imprisonment -- the continued imprisonment of this singular defendant has been seen by many as a barrier to the end of peace. And so we submit, Your Honour - and my time has run out - that there are grave questions about the jurisdiction of this Court over this relatively small incident that did not constitute a war crime, that the factors that we've indicated, the factors of the legitimacy of the operation, the relative small number of casualties, the young, inexperienced nature of the defendant, all both go to the jurisdiction of the Court as to whether this is the kind of war crime that was appropriately the subject of this Court. And also to the individual culpability of the defendant, to which I now turn to my brother who will be addressing that issue. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're also arguing that what took place did not reach the level of intensity required for an armed conflict. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: Two arguments Your Honour, one, that the general issue of the conflict, short-lived conflict, relatively small number of casualties, completely internal, with United Nations statements on all sides, did not reach the intensity, did not reach the level of armed conflict. Second, that the incidents that are the subject of this case were not sufficient to bring this incident to the level of a war crime, particularly if it grew out of a completely legitimate operation and because the defendant played this intermediate role. So both, we challenge the jurisdiction of the Court on the general issue of the Macedonian conflict, an issue which was left open by the Appellate Tribunal, and we most specifically change the jurisdiction of the Court over this, what we allege is not a war crime at all. If it was a crime, it should have been punished in Macedonia. The Macedonian government was prepared to do it when the Court took jurisdiction essentially away from it. This is much more like the kind of local crime that should be investigated locally than the kind of war crime that this Court, this Tribunal is used to hearing, Karadzic and other cases of that kind. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: Thank you, Your Honour. Nathan Dershowitz. And I would like to address specifically and I intend to address the core issues I think that Judge Robinson and Judge Meron were asking about. And specifically with respect to Judge Robinson's question as to whether had they found absolutely what the purpose of the operation was as opposed to apparently, would we be here. And the answer is: Without a doubt. And the reason for that, as I will elaborate upon, is the impropriety of that conclusion under the facts here. This Court does both, a review of the law and a review of factual conclusions which have no basis in fact, which have a material effect upon the ultimate disposition. So I will address that question specifically. With respect to Judge Meron's questions, I would like to focus upon the assumption that this Court has jurisdiction, which we do not concede, and upon its specific prior determinations to demonstrate that in this situation looking solely at Mr. Johan Tarculovski, there is no basis for this conviction. To state the obvious, the charge here was a violation of Article 7(1), in terms of the responsibility, and as this Court is well aware, it says: "A person who planned, instigated, ordered, committed -- planned, instigated, ordered, committed or otherwise aided and abetted in the planning, preparation or execution of a crime referred to in Article 2 ..." The "or" in there suggests that it should be one of the specific modes of liability. And Mr. Tarculovski was convicted of violating Count 1, murder, a violation of the laws or customs of war, under Article 3 of the Statute, for ordering, planned and instigated. And I emphasise the fact that it says "or" or "and" because as this decision is rendered, one cannot tell if the determination has been made that he was guilty of planning, as a crime, separate from instigating, separate from ordering; or whether it's a conglomeration of three, and taking bits and pieces from each, there is a conviction. To the extent to which there's a lack of clarity, we suggest that violates the rules of this Court, in terms of Article 23 and Rule 98 ter, because you need a reasoned decision. Assuming for the moment that the conjunctive means that he was convicted of each of the three, I'd like to go through that and show you that a careful - and I emphasise careful - review of the Judgement demonstrates the gross improprieties of the conviction under these circumstances. In Count 1 - now let me focus on Count 1 and the murder count - on the planning mode of liability, there is a requirement under the case law, as the Trial Chamber noted and it's supported by a number of cases, that the actus reus of planning requires that one or more persons plan or design both. Both, the preparatory and execution phase. Two, of the criminal conduct constituting the crime, and then goes on in terms of defining the mens rea. And it's in the mens rea that it talks about the accused must have acted with the intent that the crime be committed or with an awareness of the substantial likelihood that a crime will be committed in the execution of the -- of the action. So what you have is, in terms of actus reus, you have two specific elements that are required to be demonstrated, and the cases cited by the Judgement all state that the planning implies that one or several persons contemplated the commission of a crime at both, both the preparatory and the execution phase. In this situation, a review of the evidence relating to the preparatory phase shows the gaping deficiency, gaping deficiency in the evidence. The Chamber found that the operation was planned, on 10 August 2001, in direct response to the land-mine killing of eight soldiers that day. To the extent that the Prosecutor is now taking a new position, that is irrelevant. There was a very specific finding. It goes on for page -- for paragraph after paragraph, noting that this was a specific response to the killing of eight people earlier that day and the injuring of six others in the blowing up of the tank. And throughout the Judgement, the Prosecutor's submission there is a -- just pervasive confusion between the operation and the planning of a crime in violation of Article 3. The plan of an operation does not automatically equate with the planning of a crime charged. And what is very interesting here is the operation was planned on 10 August and implemented on 12 August, and there is no doubt, and I will tell you why there is no doubt, that is to weed out and capture Xhavit Hasani and others who were involved in the terrorist activities. Not only was that the Defence, that was specifically the Prosecutor's position. The Prosecutor, in its opening argument, said that Boskoski believed that Hasani was responsible for killing eight soldiers, that Hasani was hiding in Ljuboten, and that Boskoski ordered Tarculovski to conduct a search of Ljuboten for Hasani, the leader of the NLA. That's the Prosecutor's position. So that you have the Prosecutor, on page 353 of the record, taking the position that Tarculovski was ordered to go into Ljuboten to capture the terrorists because his superiors believed that the terrorists were hiding in that town. So you have both sides agreeing that the object of the plan was to capture the terrorists. This is a serious question here as to why that is not a preexisting assumption that is made by the Tribunal with respect to the planning phase. There was no direct evidence, no direct evidence that the plan or design discussed on 10 August was the indiscriminate attack on ethnic Albanians. Every single piece of direct evidence, every witness, every document, and I dare say every inference from before the facts as to what occurred at the preparatory stage, all, all, lead to the conclusion that the preparatory stage - I'm now not discussing the execution stage, I'm discussing the preparatory stage - which must be shown beyond a reasonable doubt in order for there to be a conviction for planning. You have the testimony of the witnesses. You have the documents that were introduced. You have the history of the events. You have the delay in the execution of the events. Every single piece of evidence, the whole history that the Tribunal -- the Chamber went through, in terms of what led up to the events, all deal with the NLA. All deal with the NLA what was doing in the conflict with Macedonian government. Therefore showing that it was all related to the capturing of the NLA people who were believed by the ministers and possibly the president were hiding in that town. What happened here, Your Honours, is that the Prosecution, unable to legitimately show that the plan at the preparatory stage, a prerequisite for conviction of planning, was unlawful or was even a violation of any principles of international law, argued without any evidentiary basis that the real objective was the indiscriminatory attack on ethnic Albanian. What you have, Your Honour, is this simply a sleight of hand. You have no -- no evidence that at the preparatory stage this was the objective. As we'd argued earlier, recognising the legitimacy of the goal, there were positions that the Prosecutor could have taken. They could have argued, for example, that there was a lack of concern for civilians. They could have argued that the action was disproportionate -- had a disproportionate impact on civilians. They could have argued that it was foreseeable that civilians would be killed. If they made any of those arguments, the Trial Chamber would have to have made findings as to what the law was on those subjects, and as my brother explained, there is no real law but assuming there was, the Chamber would then have to articulate what the law was, and then make findings once it articulated the law. That is a difficult process here. So instead, in answer to Judge Robinson's question, they simply made it up. If you read through the conclusions of the Court, and I will get to the specific conclusions, there is zero basis, zero basis with respect to the necessary finding of the preparatory stage for arriving at the conclusion that the Chamber arrived at, because it was necessary to circumvent the issues that we think have to be addressed by this Court. Zero basis for concluding at the preparatory stage what the objective was. What I'd like to do is jump ahead and then come back, and that is in addition to there not being any, any evidence with respect to the preparatory stage, what the Chamber did, which I believe is totally illegitimate, is to take a look at the execution phase, eliminate the preparatory stage, since you need both, eliminate the preparatory, only look at the execution, then say, On the basis of the execution phase, we now find the preparatory stage. That eliminates an element of the crime. It is improper. You must prove every element of the crime. You cannot eliminate an element of a crime because it is too difficult to prove, and under this Court's jurisprudence, you must prove both, preparatory and execution. But what I'd like to do is to go through the circumstantial evidence from what ultimately occurred and show how they improperly then used that to bootstrap an operation into the preparatory phase. Assuming you can do that properly, which I reject, let's see what they did. And the critical paragraph is paragraph 571 of the Judgement. It's most essential paragraph and it says -- let me read the whole thing because it's important: "As mentioned earlier, there is some evidence which suggests that the object of the operation, the lawful enforcement to locate and arrest or in some ways deal with NLA members also described as terrorists in the village" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you for slowing down when reading. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: -- "in some in some respects, but only in some respects, the conduct of the police in relation to the detained people who were not shot can be seen as consistent with that purpose. In most respects, however" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Dershowitz, the interpreter is asking you to speak more slowly. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: Slow down?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: I warned the interpreter before, and I apologise. The quote goes on to say that: "Other factors which demonstrate that the operation was so -- was not solely or substantially one of law enforcement or directed against the NLA includes the following ..." Then they list three factors. And I think it is important to go through each of those factors just to demonstrate that even on the basis of the circumstantial evidence, the conclusion as to the preparatory stage simply is not legitimate in terms of other findings made by the Tribunal. I'm not now talking about wrenching statements out of context. I'm now not talking about the other improprieties of saying we don't accept the military -- I mean, how do you not accept that all of the military under these circumstances, all of the other police under the circumstances, and expect Mr. Tarculovski to present a Defence? I mean, it cannot be done. The only people who have knowledge are the military and the police. If you say as a matter of category we exclude them, you have eliminated the due process rights to defend one self. You can do that by excluding all of that testimony. But let me just read the three sections. It says: "The composition of the police unit which conducted the operation, this was not composed of regular police experienced in criminal or terrorist investigation but reservists from a security agency and apparently other volunteers." The suggestion that from the composition of the force you can sort of infer guilt by -- of Johan Tarculovski is specifically inconsistent with numerous other paragraphs in the Judgement. Specifically, the Chamber finds elsewhere that it could not determine the composition of the police. It could not identify who the policemen were. It also says: "We cannot be satisfied that the Lions, Tigers and another group specifically under the control of the minister, of Minister Boskoski, was also in the town, but that doesn't eliminate that factor in consideration of reasonable doubt." But much more important, in paragraphs 492 through 496 of the Judgement, the Chamber discusses in details how and when reservists are called up, who was responsible for calling them up, how they function, how they're assigned their responsibilities, and the authority that they have. These findings destroy any inference from that cryptic paragraph. For example, the Judgement observes, in normal circumstances, all police duties are carried out by the regular police, but reserve forces were called in conditions of war or emergency situation. So the reservists were called up legitimately. It then says that the reservists are called up by Minister of Interior pursuant to an order of the president and the Security Council. It then describes in detail the responsibility of the reservists, and it continues in saying how they are acting in the full capacity as members of police or the military under those circumstances. They're ex-military people who were assigned to the police. They're assigned to the military. They're assigned for civilian defence. But the Chamber then concludes, in this respect, members of the police reserve who entered the village of Ljuboten on 12 August 2001 and those who were performing duties at police stations at the time, had all been armed, uniformed, and equipped by the polices. While it is suggested that a few of them had criminal records, this is not established by the evidence. And then it goes on saying it was not established. They then go on to have a discussion, in paragraph 497, of this private security force, and they say that there was a contract entered into between the minister of interior and this private security force, Kometa. It goes on to describe, in 497, how these people were considered active reservists. And it goes on, the equipment also -- the evidence also reveals that persons sent to Kometa were equipped earlier. The Chamber finds: "These events indicate that the men sent from Kometa were on the MOI list of police reserves who, on reporting to the ministry for reserve duty, either as a volunteer or having been personally summoned, have been accepted for active service as a member of the police reserve." So having found that Kometa and having found that there was no criminal record on behalf of these people, having found that they're called up by the minister of interior, that there had to be an order from the president, how do you reach the conclusion that Johan Tarculovski somehow implicitly was involved in this preparatory stage on the basis of that? I suggest it simply cannot be done. I'd love to hear the Prosecutor explain to this Tribunal, in light of the other findings by the Chamber, as to why that supports the notion that, that at the preparatory stage, Johan Tarculovski intended to, and designed a plan for the random indiscriminately attacking members of the ethnic Albanian community. It can't happen. You can't get there from here, in light of the findings that had been made. Seconds it says: "The operation was led by Tarculovski, who had no experience in criminal or terrorist activities, and those normal positions and duties would not rank him as leader of the group." Now bear in mind there is a finding that he was ordered to carry out this operation. That is not a condemnation of the person ordered to carry it out. It is a condemnation of the people who ordered him to carry it out. In no way does that show culpability on the part of the lower level person who is told to go in and to try to find the terrorists to suggest that he lacked experience. Who is chargeable with that? Is the person ordered to go in chargeable because he lacks experience? Or is the person who orders him to do it chargeable with the fact that he lacks experience? Finally, what the Tribunal does, the Chamber does, is it then goes through the events that occurred in the actual village in order to show that this demonstrated what had previously been planned. And I'm emphasising planning. The same problem exists in every one of the other counts here, and if I had time, I would go through every one in meticulous detail to show the absolute lack of evidence here. Let me just point out. The Prosecutor keeps saying, We don't respect the findings in the Judgement. I just want to emphasise we understand the findings in the Judgement. We are challenging the findings in the Judgement because they are not based on any evidence. There are no citations to the record for critical conclusions. Let me give you just a couple of examples. They say, We find that the military went through as one unit. No citation in the record for that finding. No basis for that finding. They then say, We find that Johan Tarculovski led. That is said four or five times in the Judgement. Never is there a citation. If you look, not one time when it comes to that conclusion is there a citation for that conclusion from the record. The Prosecutor will then cite to the Judgement, not to the record, in order to support the conclusion because the evidence doesn't exist for purposes of the conclusion that's arrived at. So if you just simply want to pronounce conclusions, what do you need a trial for? The purpose of the trial is to produce the evidence. The purpose of a Judgement is to rely upon the evidence produced, the documents. Sur you can make certain and we challenge some of the inferences that were drawn. I'm now not talking about the inferences. I'm talking about findings. Whether there's any, any evidence to support the critical findings with respect, in this situation, to the planning phase. With respect to what actually occurred, the last paragraph of that -- last part of that paragraph is extremely interesting. It says that they -- they rely upon the fact that the police did not proceed along all roads in the village and entered -- and didn't enter and search all houses or all houses occupied by ethnic Albanians. Instead, the operation was essentially confined to houses that could be readily reached from the main road. Now, let's look at that for one moment. What have you is the houses that they entered. They entered one house which had ten to 15 men in one part, women in the other part. What inference is to be drawn from going into one house? That this is a random attack? Or is it that it was a specifically laser focussed operation to try to find a person who they believed was in that house at the time? It then goes to a second house. They don't go in. Five people run away. Three are killed. There is no indication or the Court could not find one way or the other with respect to those, but it is not unreasonable to find for purposes of finding guilt beyond a reasonable doubt that they were members of the NLA. So that doesn't show a random indiscriminate attack upon civilians. It shows a focussed attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Meron, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I think that the President asked a key question, which was partly answered by Mr. Alan Dershowitz but it is quite important and I would like some further argument on your part on that. The President asked whether the conflict that we are discussing has reached the threshold that would enable us to qualify it, to characterise it as an internal armed conflict. In Tadic case, which I mentioned earlier, in paragraph 70, there is a very interesting discussion of the intensity requirements which would apply in order for a conflict to qualify as either internal or international conflict. And then, in another paragraph, I believe, 78, the Appeals Chamber in the Tadic case, the subject matter jurisdiction of the international Tribunal should extend to both internal and international conflict. I understood that the argument of Mr. Dershowitz was this did not reach the intensity required for an internal armed conflict, but further argument on that from you would be useful. And I would like also the Prosecutor in due course to explain to us why the threshold was reached. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: Judge Meron, let me --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOUDREAULT
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may interrupt for a moment. The appellant never raised the issue whether there was an internal conflict or not. In his appeal brief and his reply, he simply accepted that there was an internal armed conflict. This new position taken today is an impermissible attempt to expand the appeal and should be ignored. Thank you. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The procedural point you make is correct, but if the Appeals Chamber considers that it is important, we can hear it. And if we have to make allowances in terms of time, because of lack of preparation then we'll do so. Mr. Alan Dershowitz, in relation to that particular point, you mentioned that the Prosecutor had conceded that the events in Northern Ireland would not, in their view, have reached the level of intensity required for an armed conflict. Where is that to be found, that concession? MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: I think, Your Honour, may I have a moment while my brother continues --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: -- and I'll find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: Judge Meron, let me answer the question -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Also to continue the President's point, if this is a jurisdictional matter pertaining to our competence, then whether this was raised or not in the briefs would not be definitive. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: That was one of my two answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Judge Guney has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] Mr. Dershowitz, you insisted on the fact that the police operation was a regular operation. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: I have to change channels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Okay, I repeat. [Interpretation] You insisted on saying -- you insisted on -- MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: What channel is -- if I could inquire what channel --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English booth? 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Number 4. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: Four, thank you. I apologise. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: Your Honour while my brother is looking, may I respond a give you the citation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, please allow Judge Guney to ask his question. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You insisted on the fact that the police operation was a regular police operation. Elsewhere, you also said that this was an operation which called for reserve forces. This is somewhat contradictory. If this was a police operation, a regular police operation, normally speaking you should not have called for reservists. So I would seek your opinion on this point. Thank you for clarifying this point for me. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: Your Honour, I never indicated it was a regular police operation. What I did indicate is that it was an operation conducted in the normal course under the specific provisions of the Statute which the Court found which included reservists. In other words, when there was a conflict, whether a large conflict, a small conflict, but a conflict, there was the right to call up reservists and make the reservists function as part of the military, police, the civil defence. And the Court found that they had been called up. So they were integrated into the operation. For example, the people in the tank who were killed, the day -- on the 10th of August, police -- I mean, military, most of those were reservists. In other words, when you had a conflict -- a situation, you had the right to call up reservists and integrate them into and make them part of and function as the regular police and as the military. And the Court made that finding. So I'm not saying normal, regular police. What I'm saying is, under the police, power, responsibility, who they can call up, they called up the -- they called up people and they used regular police, regular police were used. How many, who, and what, the Court says, We don't know. We cannot figure out. The Hermelin, for example, was regular police. Many of the people were regular police. But, again, Your Honour, the point I am emphasising is that you need to make a finding. It is a necessary, under your jurisprudence, a necessary finding in order to support, for example, planning, that there was a preparation to commit the crime. Not that the crime occurred. A separate responsibility. The inference that is suggested that since this was reserve therefore it was a plan, one is inconsistent with the finding as to when reserves are used, in general; two, who called up the reserve; and three, who is available to be used by, assuming it was Tarculovski who actually led it, who was he able to choose from? There's no suggestion he called up reserves. There's no suggestion he called -- there's a suggestion flat out inconsistent with the Judgement, other parts of the Judgement. Flat out inconsistent that he selected these people from Kometa. But the Judgement says in other places, in dealing with the Boskoski section, how Kometa had a contract, how they were called up, who called them up. That was all the minister. Not a low level person walking around saying, I want you, and you and you. That's not what the facts are under these circumstances. Judge Meron, in response to your question, you're making an assumption, or at least in the question there is an assumption that I believe is invalid. The assumption is that if there is an armed conflict somewhere, everything that takes place is necessarily governed only by the armed conflict rules and regulations. That's the first assumption. And I question that assumption, because, for example, if this was a -- let's -- military operation, but they found people in a town and they went into the town for some other reason, I wonder whether that's governed by your prior determinations. But, second, and more significantly, the question then becomes assuming -- and I am for purposes of my argument assuming that this is covered by your jurisprudence, the question -- which we don't agree with, but the question then becomes if they -- if there are NLA in the town and he is charged with preparing, among other things, to engage in that activity, what rules then apply under those circumstances? Yes, assuming there is jurisprudence -- there's jurisdiction, the question then becomes: What happens when you want to go into a town, legitimately? Can you? The Prosecutor seems to suggest no. Because they give -- they create not only a terrorist veto; in other words, the more the terrorists engage in activity. What is terror? By definition is to create a feeling of terror on the part of the civilian population. To then say the terrorists succeeded in creating apprehension among the civilian population - therefore, you cannot go in and challenge the terrorists - is, to me, that terrorists have won. What I'd like to do is just spend a few moments just dealing with what is the other core deficiency within the record. And that is the -- the conclusion is one he planned, and I think I've demonstrated that the essential element of planning simply was never shown beyond a reasonable doubt. But if you go to the other conclusions that exist in this case which are the conclusions which supposedly support the Judgement, you have the conclusions that he also instigated and ordered the -- not the operation, not the operation, the crimes. The Article 3 violations that he ordered, for example, the murders. That's what is required in order to make a determination that he ordered the crimes. You have an extremely, extremely large leap to determine not based on any evidence that he actually was with the police as they go through the town. I suggest that if you read the critical evidence, which is M-037's testimony, nobody can read that testimony -- which is the only testimony credited for showing that he was in the town. You cannot reach the conclusion, certainly not beyond a reasonable doubt, that he actually was with the group of people that went through the town. But assuming through those leaps of logic you can get there, ordering is a different crime. He had to have ordered the murders. He had to have ordered the murders. He did not commit the murders himself. He had to have ordered them. And what you have here is no evidence that he ordered any of these murders. As I said, you don't even have evidence that he was at the Jusufi house, but assuming he was there, and somebody saw somebody closing a door and shot, what -- how do you get from somebody being shot to his ordering that person to be shot? There's a leap. There is no evidence, certainly no evidence beyond a reasonable doubt as to that. Go to the second incident, where the man is attempting to futilely escape. You have an indication of one person said, Let him go and we'll shoot him. No evidence that that was Tarculovski. In fact, you do have evidence that some people tried to stop the abuse that was taking place. But under the evidence in the case, Tarculovski wasn't there at the time. Under the only person credited with the time-line, and let me tell you the time-line is -- is -- if you look at it carefully you will see that the indictment has a time-line at 8.00 for the first killing, I think 11.00 or 11.30 for the second, and 12.00 for the other, but in order to be able say that it was only Tarculovski and only his group, the Judgement leaves out that time-line for purposes of finding the guilt and simply says later, later, later, leaving the impression that the first one took place at 8.00, where the evidence all is that Tarculovski wasn't even in the town at that time. The second one, they say, Later, which is a problem because when is later? Two and a half, three and a half hours later? Then have you to have evidence to show he was still there. And the next one is later, you need evidence of that. But they simply eliminate that by sort of condensing it and using vague language. But going to the second one, if he is not there, and if he is there, did he order them to shoot? This sounds like a -- an intentional murder, a totally inappropriate murder. Why is that laid on his shoulders because somebody -- because an improper determination is made in a use of a word that he led. If you are talking about actually being present and the person who was there and gave the order, then have you ordering. With respect to instigating, you have to have something specific, that indicates instigating. The third murder that he is convicted of, the Chamber says, We don't know when it occurred, how it occurred, who it occurred by. The only evidence referred to is that the son and one other person said that in prison, later, they had heard that he was shot by the police. That is the sole evidence I have been able to find to support the claim that even the police did it. But to suggest that Johan Tarculovski is responsible for having ordered that person shot when he don't even know if he was there and you certainly have no evidence of an order is, I suggest, under the requirements grossly inappropriate. You need to find guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. You have to have evidence. And I understand, with all due respect to this Chamber, that certain broad issues are the types of issues that are much more interesting. But going through a factual evaluation is, as I have found going through it, tedious. But if you simply have pronouncements without any support and inconsistencies and no basis for the determination, as Judge Meron once said in an article that he wrote, due process has to be consistent with the process of the jurisdiction of the Tribunals. What is the most basic element of due process? Is that someone is not convicted in the absence of evidence. That there is a presumption of innocence, which applies in these situations, that guilt be established beyond a reasonable doubt. Simply announcing, announcing, He led the group, we believe he was there at all times, is not guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. If you want to write a report about what happened, and you try to put the pieces together to make a logical story, do that. But that's not a Judgement consistent with the requirements of this Tribunal and it has to be based on evidence beyond a reasonable doubt. And what I'm suggesting to this Tribunal is superficially a certain statement is made and, it could be made 30 times in the Judgement, if there is nothing to support it, if the inference is not allowed, if there isn't evidence, if there's no evidence beyond a reasonable doubt, that's a fundamental violation of due process. I'd like to just end on -- on the last point that we make in our -- in our presentation and it has to do with the sentence that was imposed. And under one of the provisions in the Macedonian code - I believe it is Article 40 - under extraordinary circumstances it is appropriate -- in extraordinary mitigating circumstances it is appropriate to impose a lesser sentence than the one that is quoted in the Judgement as reflecting the Macedonian law. That allows under these circumstances for reduction of a sentence down to five years, or a minimum sentence of five years. The Chamber simply ignored that -- that provision. Made reference to mitigating circumstances but ignored that provision. And if there has ever been a situation where you can examine it in terms of extraordinary mitigating circumstances, where you have someone who the Chamber held was honourable, there was nothing that reflects any impropriety on his part, you see a long range of activities that -- of his never engaging in anything. He's trustworthy. He's reliable. And everybody else, everybody else has been given amnesty, and the granting of the amnesty was in order to encourage the part -- conflicting forces to get together, to be united, to be part of a joint government as they are at the present time, all of that suggests that under these circumstances, any sentence which doesn't recognise that and a 12-year sentence under the circumstances was excessive and well beyond any propriety. Being the only one in jail at the present time and all of amnesties suggest that we should have his sentence reduced significantly. If there are no more questions, I will reserve my time for -- if there is any time, for later and answer questions later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Alan Dershowitz, you're going provide some information. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: Your Honours, the issue of Northern Ireland was presented by testimony, and -- briefing in the Defence of Mr. Boskoski.
