utterances.speaker: MR. BOUDREAULT
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I will be addressing Grounds 1 and 2 of the appeal. My colleague Laurel Baig will be addressing Grounds 3 to 5. Nadia Shihata will then address Grounds 6 and 7. Before I begin, please let me introduce a person that has been inadvertently omitted, and that is our Case Manager, Colin Nawrot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Obviously the most important person.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOUDREAULT
utterances.text: Yes. At the outset, I will deal with the issue of the existence of an internal armed conflict. As mentioned earlier, this issue was not briefed in the appellants brief. Further, at paragraph 85 of his appellant's brief, the appellant even accepted that there was an armed conflict. This was noted in paragraph 27 of the Prosecution's response, and there was no reply on this point. Turning to the question itself. Our answer is that the Trial Chamber very carefully assessed the law and the evidence before concluding the conflict between the NLA and the Macedonian forces constituted an internal armed conflict. And this is at Trial Judgement paragraph 175 to 292. The Chamber first identified the relevant test as outlined in Tadic decision. This is at Trial Judgement paragraph 175. It identified the two relevant criteria; first, the intensity of the conflict, and second, the organisations -- organisation of the parties to the armed conflict. At paragraph 177 to 206, the Chamber outlined the law and the relevant factors going to these two criteria. From paragraph 208 to 249, the Chamber discusses the evidence as to the intensity of the conflict between the NLA and the Macedonian forces to conclude in the end that the conflict had reached the intensity of an armed conflict. The Chamber analysed all the events in Macedonia from January 2001 to October 2001. And that's at paragraph 212 to 228 of the Trial Judgement. The Chamber found that there was territory controlled by the NLA, dozens of villages. That's at Trial Judgement 242. It noted that there was large mobilisation carried out by the Macedonia army and the police to counter the offensive of the NLA, and a large number of Macedonian soldiers and police were sent to the northern parts of Macedonia, where the NLA threat was the greatest. There were several orders of the president to carry out these mobilisation in the evidence. Third, a great deal of modern weaponry was used by the Macedonian force. These included fixed-wing aircrafts that bombed and rocketed NLA positions, helicopters, heavy artillery, tanks, rocket-propelled grenades, machine-guns, and mines. Fourth, there were casualties on all sides, and even though it is difficult to -- to find the precise number of NLA casualties, the important point is that there were casualties on both sides. Fifth, the conflict led to the internal displacement of thousands of ethnic Albanians and ethnic Macedonians. Many thousands also fled the country. Sixth --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Paragraph 248, we're told there was extensive displacement of persons from their homes and villages, at least 64.000 of whom became refugees, and 70.000 of whom were internally displaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOUDREAULT
utterances.text: Indeed. Indeed, Your Honour. The sixth element relating to the intensity of the conflict relates to its protracted nature. The conflict started in January 2001 and continued on until -- until the autumn of 2001. The last element noted by the Trial Chamber that I would like to mention is the extent of the damage resulting from the conflict, and this is discussed at Trial Judgement paragraph 241, 241. For further references, I would invite you to turn to our final trial brief in this case at paragraph 396 to 429, on the issue of the intensity of the armed conflict. There we list all the evidence going to that question, evidence which was accepted by the Trial Chamber to find that the intensity of the conflict had reached that of an armed conflict. Now, all these conclusions of the Trial Chamber were based on the correct law and they have not been shown to be unreasonable. These are our basic submissions in this regard. However, if Your Honours would require more information on this, we would be happy to provide them in additional written submissions. I will now turn to Ground 1 of the appeal. Ground 1 should be rejected for the reasons given in our response brief. In addition, I would point to your decision of 12 October 2009, in the Karadzic case, at paragraph 36 and 39, where Your Honours explain that the scope of the Tribunal's jurisdiction is entirely contingent upon the Statute and that than this jurisdiction can only be limited by a Security Council resolution. Here, the Statute is clear. There is no exception to the Tribunal's jurisdiction for individuals purporting to act in self-defence against terrorists. Further, there is no Security Council resolution expressly or even implicitly limiting the Tribunal's jurisdiction in respect of the events in the Republic of Macedonia in 2001. The Tribunal thus had jurisdiction to try the appellant, and Ground 1 of his appeal should be rejected. Turning to Ground 2(A), the applicable law. Your Honours, there are no uncertainties as to the laws and customs of war that applied here. The Trial Chamber found that the conflict between the Macedonian forces and the NLA constituted an internal armed conflict, a finding, as I just mentioned, that the appellant did not even challenge. The existence of an internal armed conflict triggered the application of a number of IHL rules which had to be respected by all parties to the conflict. These rules included Common Article 3, and the prohibition on wanton destruction or devastation not justified by military necessity. Whether the Macedonian forces were acting in self-defence against terrorists has no relevance to the applicable jus in bello. It's a basic principle that once there is an armed conflict, the rule of IHL apply equally to all parties to the conflict. This connection, I would refer to our response brief paragraph 30 and 32. And note that this principle was reiterated by the Security Council in its resolution of 21 March 2001, dealing specifically with the Macedonian situation. That is Exhibit 1D230 at paragraph 7 of the resolution, where the Security Council states: "Further underlines the requirement for all parties to act with restraint and full respect for international humanitarian law and human rights." The appellant argues that the applicable law is "hotly debated" with respect to state response to terrorism. However, the only uncertainties he refers to relate to jus ad bellum issues, whether states can lawfully use force to respond to terrorists operating from other states. That is what is discussed in the article of Beck and Arend to which the appellant refers. There are no uncertainties as to the jus in bello; as soon as there's an armed conflict, all parties are bound by applicable humanitarian law. This is also recognised by Beck and Arend which state that self-defence actions against terrorism are not exempt from the humanitarian rules applicable to armed conflict. I would also refer you to the decision of the United States Supreme Court in Hamdan v. Rumsfeld, decision of 2006, where the majority states at page 66 to 68 that: "Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions applies even to an armed conflict with terrorists such as al Qaeda." I would also refer you to the report of the United Nations fact-finding mission on the Gaza conflict of 15th September 2009, the Goldstone Report, at paragraph 270. So there are no uncertainties that the provisions of Common Article 3 apply to all parties in any armed conflict. That was long -- that was the situation long before August 2001. The provisions of Common Article 3 were found to reflect the most elementary considerations of humanity and to apply to all parties in armed conflict without any exceptions or limitations. In addition to the authorities mentioned in our response brief, Your Honours recalled this most recently in the Mrksic appeal Judgement at paragraph 70, and in your decision of 9 July 2009 in the Karadzic case at paragraph 23 to 26. The appellant also argues that the provision of Common Article 3 should not apply in the present situation because the NLA hid among civilians and made it difficult for the Macedonian forces to distinguish who was actively involved in the hostilities. What the appellant is asking is asking the Appeals Chamber to change the law, and create an exception to a fundamental rule of IHL. There are many problems with this. First, it is for states to change the law, either through treaties or through changing practice and opinio juris. Second, while it may not always be easy to distinguish fighters and civilians, this is not a new problem. It is common to many wars, to all guerrilla wars, to many internal and international armed conflicts. It does not mean that the parties should be exempted from attempting to make distinctions or from the application of Common Article 3. To hold otherwise would render IHL meaningless. States could evade their IHL obligations simply by using the terrorist label for all groups with whom they are engaged in armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: For the benefit of the public, I think it is preferable to say international humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOUDREAULT
utterances.text: Sure. Thank you, President. So, states could evade their international humanitarian law obligations simply by using the terrorist label for all groups with whom they are engaged in armed conflict. Civilians taking no active part in the hostilities and persons hors de combat would lose all protection. These dangers are all too well illustrated by the present case. Contrary to the appellant's assertion, the fact that Common Article 3 applies to all parties in all armed conflicts does not eviscerate a state's right to use force against so-called terrorists. States can, of course, attack fighting members of armed groups once they are located, and such actions may result in some civilian victims. The civilian victims will be lawful as long as they are collateral and proportionate damage to an otherwise lawful attack. And by proportionate, we mean, of course, the ratio between the military advantage gained and the casualty to the civilian population, and not the proportionate notion that is applicable in jus ad bellum in relation to Article 51, the right to self-defence. This is a completely different issue. So civilians will be lawful when -- civilian casualties will be lawful when they're collateral and proportionate damage to an otherwise lawful attack. They will also be lawful when they were taking an active part in the hostilities at the time. So it is clear that the law recognises that not all civilians are unlawful. Not all civilian victims are unlawful, sorry. In the case at hand, the civilian casualties were not taking an active part in the hostilities and were not simply collateral and proportional damage, as will be discussed further by my colleague, Laurel Baig. For all these reasons, Ground 2(A) should be dismissed. With respect to Ground 2(B), I would simply refer Your Honours to our response brief at paragraph 35, where we explain that Article 7(4) of the Statute very clearly states that acting pursuant to a order does not relieve someone of criminal liability, but may be considered in sentencing. Your Honours, unless there are any questions, this would conclude our submissions on -- in response to Grounds 1 and 2 of the appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Boudreault. Yes, Ms. Baig.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Laurel Baig, and I will respond to Grounds 3 to 5 of Tarculovski's appeal. These grounds focus on the Trial Chamber's evaluation of the evidence, factual findings, and legal conclusions. Tarculovski's conviction for planning, ordering and instigating the crimes of murder cruel treatment and wanton destruction were based on the totality of the evidence and on the correct law. The appellant fails to meet the standard of review on appeal. He fails to show that the Trial Chamber's careful factual findings are in any way unreasonable. He fails to demonstrate any legal error. For these reasons, Grounds 3 to 5 of the appeal should be dismissed. Your Honours, I plan to take you quickly through the events of the 12th of August. My goal is to put the appellant's arguments back into the context from which he has tried to isolate them. After this overview, I will then move to respond to three of his arguments in more detail, concerning the protected status of the victims, the illegal objective of the operation, and its planning. The Trial Chamber found that on the 12th of August, 2001, Johan Tarculovski led a group of 60 to 70 uniformed members of the Macedonian police reserve in an attack against the ethnically Albanian village of Ljuboten. They murdered three unarmed civilians, brutally assaulted 13 men, and destroyed 12 homes. The Prosecution proved that Tarculovski planned, ordered and instigated the attack, the primary purpose of which was to retaliate against the civilian population of Ljuboten for the arm -- for the villagers perceived support for the Albanian National Liberation Army, the NLA. At paragraph 572 of the Judgement, the Trial Chamber links this retaliatory attack against civilians in the village to the land-mine explosion which occurred two days before, killing eight Macedonian soldiers. Two of the dead were from Tarculovski's home town of Ljubanci, which is the ethnically Macedonian town adjoining Ljuboten. Tarculovski was close to one of the men who died. This incident occurred approximately ten kilometres away, and it was believed that those responsible fled to Ljuboten village after the incident. In order to assist Your Honours, I'd like to refer to two exhibits. The first one I've given to the usher in hard copy, because it is under seal, and I'm not going to show it on the screen. It's a printout from the e-court record. And I would be grateful if the registry officer could pass it out. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: Your Honour, can I be told what it is so that I can look at it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: Yes, it's coming from the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You'll tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you bring it also to my colleagues on the Defence. My purpose in showing this picture is quite simple, Your Honours. It is to orient you in the village of Ljuboten. In this picture you can see that the village is a populated one. The Trial Chamber estimated about 3.000 inhabitants, and to get your sense of direction, you can notice the mosque on the top left-hand corner of the image. I'm also going to refer to Exhibit P411, and I'm going to show that one on the screen because it is a public exhibit. Is it showing now? This exhibit -- Your Honours, this picture is a partial map of Ljuboten. It was generated by the International Management Group, which is a European non-governmental agency. The reason that I'm using it is that this map usefully illustrates the Judgement because the houses where the crimes occurred are marked on the map by number, which corresponds to Prosecution Exhibit P410, and the map therefore allows you to follow the events through the village as the police group progresses through it. I should point out before I begin to use it that this is a partial map. So it -- it does not include all of the houses, for example, that you can see in the photo that I have distributed. It only indicates the houses that were damaged. The map contains other information such as the level of damage, and includes houses that were damaged on other days not relevant to this Judgement. But as I take you through this presentation, I'm going highlight the relevant information for you, so that you can follow along and see where exactly the houses were, where the crimes occurred. Your Honours, in the morning of the 12th of August, following some initial mortar shelling by the army, Tarculovski led the police into the village at approximately 8.00 a.m. The Hermelin armoured personnel carrier entered the village soon after and was there to support the attack. It is the Trial Chamber's finding that Tarculovski personally led the police operation and was with the group of police as they moved through the village. That can be found at Judgement paragraph 564. This finding was based on the totality of the evidence, including M-37 who was referred to by my learned friend, but also on other evidence of Tarculovski's leadership, including his own admission to the commission, which can be found in Prosecution Exhibit P397.01 and.02. In that admission, he says that he selected the men, armed them, and was with the group as they went through the village. I'll touch on other relevant findings to this issue as I go through. Your Honours, I'm now going to annotate the map that's before you to show you the route of the police through the village as set out in the Judgement. Tarculovski's police first stopped at the home of Elmaz Jusufi, and you can see that as the blue circle on the map. It's house number 137 and co-related to P410. That's where the name comes from. On that morning, the Jusufi family heard a loud explosion. Rami Jusufi ran to the front door where he was shot and killed by the police. The Chamber found that he was a civilian who was taking no active part in the hostilities. Tarculovski's police made no effort to find this out. They shot him. They did not enter the house. Instead, they set the Jusufi's car and other property on fire. The police then burnt five other houses in the vicinity. I have marked these again with Xs on your map. Tarculovski's police proceeded down that same street, towards the east of the village, along with the Hermelin APC which contained gasoline or other incendiary materials used to start the fires to burn the homes. When they reached the neighbourhood near the mosque, which I have now marked, they burned four more houses. You can the mosque again in the upper left corner of the photo, and that can give you a bit of orientation and connection between the map and the photo. You need to turn the photo upside down to match up the lines. Tarculovski's police then moved to Adem Ametovski's house, house number 205, and it's now marked with a blue circle on your screen. The police fired at a basement window and ten men who were hiding there came out waving a white flag of surrender. The police found three others hiding in the neighbour's house. They took their money, their valuables and their identity cards. Ametovski's house was the only compound that was searched in the whole village, but no weapons or any other military equipment were found by the police. Tarculovski and his police detained the 13 men in the front yard of Ametovski's house. They repeatedly and brutally beat the detainees with their weapons, punching them and kicking them. One policeman carved a cross in the back of one of the men. Another shot Aziz Bajrami in his hand. His son, Sulejman, was hit or kicked in the head. The police allowed him to move a few metres away before they shot him to death. Ten of the men detained at Adem Ametovski's house were then marched barefoot through the village towards the police check-point at Brace's house, which is just off the top of the map. Again, at Brace's house they suffered further cruel treatment, including beatings so severe that some of the men lost consciousness. Two elderly men were left behind in police custody at Adem Ametovski's house. One of them, Muharem Ramadani, was shot and killed by the police. The Trial Chamber found again that there was no evidence that any of these men had any affiliation with the NLA. None were wearing uniforms or insignia. No weapons were found in their possession. Moreover, all of them, at the time that they were beaten or killed, were in the custody of the police and were, therefore, taking no active part in the hostilities. Finally, Your Honours, a bit farther along the road, Tarculovski's police destroyed three more homes. Three men were killed in the field near these houses, but the Trial Chamber could not exclude the possibility that the fire may have come from the army. Moreover, the Trial Chamber entertained a reasonable doubt as whether these men may have been taking an active part in the hostilities. It acquitted accordingly, but it did not make any finding that they were terrorists, as suggested by my learned friends this morning. Tarculovski and his police then returned to Brace's house, where they rejoined the ten prisoners. The final tally for this retaliatory attack against the civilians of Ljuboten: 3 murdered, 13 cruelly treated and 12 homes wantonly destroyed. This was not a legitimate police operation. This was an attack on a civilian village. I'd like to respond to three of the appellant's main arguments. I am going to turn off the map now, but should it became important later on in our discussion, I can turn it back on. First I'd like to speak about the protected status of the victims in this case. The Trial Chamber carefully considered the evidence and the arguments of the parties about the civilian status of these victims. It assessed each victim and the evidence surrounding it and reached reasonable conclusions. Where it had any doubt that one of the victims might have been taking an active part in the hostilities, for example, when they heard evidence that they might have been firing at the police, the Chamber acquitted. And I would refer to you paragraph 348 of the Judgement. Where there was no doubt that the victims of murder or cruel treatment were civilians taking no active part in the hostilities, the Trial Chamber properly convicted. And here, Your Honours, I would like to highlight the fact that all but one of the victims for which Tarculovski was convicted were in the custody of the police at the time that they were assaulted or killed. These crimes did not happen as part of a legitimate operation. What is the legitimate purpose of beating, of killing people who are already in your custody? In this circumstance, even if these people were fighting members of the NLA, they would still have been hors de combat and would thus have been protected by Common Article 3. The fact of detention makes the protected status of the detained persons obvious to everyone, including the perpetrators of the crimes. The only victim who was not in detention was Rami Jusufi, and he was the first blue circle. He was killed in the doorway of his family home, while he was unarmed, wearing jeans and a white T-shirt. The Chamber found that the evidence did not support a finding that he was anything other than an unarmed civilian. In finding that the police shooters had the required mens rea for the killing, at paragraph 312 of the Judgement, the Trial Chamber noted that they shot from close range, that he was dressed in civilian clothing, that he was unarmed, and that he posed no resistance to the police. Your Honours, you heard the suggestion this morning that there some sort of continuum of civilian-ness. This is not so. The status of the victim is a fundamental concept in international humanitarian law. The principle of distinction rests on a clear division between military personnel and objects on one hand, and civilians and civilian objects on the other. This line is not blurry. It is clear. Common Article 3 protects person taking no active part in hostilities. In a non-international armed conflict, such as this one, this would exclude members of the state armed forces and fighters belonging to an organised armed group that's in armed conflict with the state, unless they have laid down their arms or been placed hors de combat. In contrast, Your Honours, a person does not lose his civilian status and Common Article 3 protection when he merely supports an armed group. As this Chamber explained in the Strugar Appeals Judgement at paragraph 177, there are many ways that a civilian can indirectly participate in the hostilities, for example, by expressing sympathy, participating in supporting activities, providing food and other supplies, et cetera. In connection this discussion I'd also like to draw your attention to the recent ICRC interpretive guidance on the concept of direct participation in hostilities. This study provides a detailed explanation of the concept and is based on extensive expert consultation. According to the ICRC's interpretive guidance, in non-international armed conflict, a person only becomes a member of an organised group under IHL when they perform a continuous combat function. This makes them functionally equivalent to the armed forces of the state. Other supporters of armed groups remain civilians and retain their protection. The Chamber notes in the Trial Judgement that there were some 1.000 members of the NLA who merely provided non-military support. Although affiliated with the NLA in some way, these individuals would still be civilians under IHL and they would retain their protection against direct attack. In any event, Your Honours, in this case, there was simply no credible evidence that Rami Jusufi was a member of the NLA. The appellant has failed to show any error in the Trial Chamber's assessment of his status or in the status of any of the other victims who were in detention. I'd like to move now to the object of the attack. The appellant argues that this was a legitimate attack, an operation aimed at rooting out NLA terrorists in the village. The Trial Chamber carefully considered and rejected these arguments which were squarely before it at trial. It found that the predominant object of the attack was to retaliate against civilians of Albanian ethnicity in the village for the actions of the NLA because the villagers were thought to have harboured or supported them. This retaliation was to serve as a warning to other villagers as to the consequences of support for the NLA. The Trial Chamber acknowledged, at paragraph 140, that there were potentially legitimate reasons for the police to enter the village of Ljuboten because of a suspected NLA presence there. But this acknowledgment of a potentially legitimate law enforcement goal does not justify the type of criminal and retaliatory attack that I've just described, that the Chamber found out was carried out and planned out by Tarculovski and his police under that -- the police under his charge that day. This was not a legitimate attack that went wrong. It was not the acts of a few rogue individual police officers. This was intended to be retaliation against the civilians. It was meant to send a warning. It was aimed at persons of Albanian ethnicity, without any reference to any actual connection with the NLA. In reaching its conclusion that this was an illegitimate purpose, at paragraph 572 of the Judgement, the Trial Chamber listed a series of relevant factors that my learned friend discussed this morning. In particular, the Trial Chamber looked at what happened that day, looked at the criminal actions of the police, including killing Albanian men who posed no threat, inflicting violence on detainees, setting fire to and firing at houses, stealing valuables from the detained men and women. This is not legitimate law enforcement, Your Honours. In the Chamber's view, these events directly contradict the purpose of the operation stated by Tarculovski of searching identified houses for terrorists. That's Trial Judgement 558, where the Trial Chamber explicitly rejects this proposition. I would also refer Your Honours to the finding that what was done by the police was done in the presence of their leader, Tarculovski. In the Trial Chamber's finding, at paragraph 565, this is a significant and reliable guide as to what was intended as the object of the operation. This is common sense. In that -- in that same paragraph, paragraph 572, the Chamber also looked at the composition of the force and the route of the attack, which I've just shown you on the map. The Chamber noted that the police were not there searching all houses or even all houses of ethnic Albanians. They only searched one house. They barely strayed from the main road. They were not searching for anyone. On the totality of the evidence, the Trial Chamber was correct to conclude that the object of the attack was retaliation against the Albanian civilians. It was entitled to conclude, as it did at paragraph 576, that the crimes were intended by Tarculovski, or, alternatively, that he was aware of the substantial likelihood that these crimes would occur in the execution of his operation. He has failed to show any error in this reasoning. Finally, I'd like to touch on planning. Contrary to what the appellant has argued, the Trial Chamber was correct to find that Tarculovski planned the attack. To clarify for a moment the elements of this mode of responsibility, the law of this Tribunal requires planning conduct with either direct intent to commit the crimes, or with an awareness of a substantial likelihood that the acts or omissions planned will result in crimes. It is not legally required, as the appellant suggests, that the plan be both the preparatory and execution phases. There's no line of distinction where you consider only preparation and then only execution. This language can be found in some trial judgements. It appears to be a remnant coming from the Akayesu trial decision, but the Appeals Chamber has never taken this approach. And I would refer you, for example, to Kordic Appeals Judgement, paragraph 26, which sets out the actus reus of planning. Finally, as we have explained in detail in our brief, it is not required --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- you refer to --

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: To Kordic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I have it here. Your Honour, Kordic says: "The actus reus of planning requires that one or more persons design the criminal conduct constituting one or more statutory crimes that are later perpetrated. It is sufficient to demonstrate that the planning was a factor substantially contributing to such conduct." And that is on the actus reus in relation to the mens rea, which I'm just about to speak about. The mens rea for these modes of responsibility is established if the perpetrator acted with direct intent at paragraph 29, or indirect intent --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you for slowing down when reading.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: -- at paragraph 30. So as we've --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And your point is that that makes no distinction between the preparatory and execution phases.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAIG
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is correct. However, in this case, as I'm going to detail in a moment, the facts of this case show that there was ample planning for this crime or for these crimes, and that this happened, as the Trial Chamber found, with either the direct intent or the indirect intent, that is, the awareness of the substantial likelihood that the crimes would occur. As we explained in our brief, it's not required that the plan be to commit the crime. Otherwise, indirect intent for planning would be impossible. Your Honour, to answer your question on the facts, this coordinated attack did not and could not have happened by accident. The Trial Chamber's conclusion that the attack was planned is well grounded in the evidence, and in the Trial Chamber's findings. The findings support Tarculovski's conviction for planning and can be usefully grouped under three headings. First, pattern; second, preparation; and third, cooperation with the army. As I have already mentioned, the Chamber placed emphasis on the pattern of crimes that took place, the repetition of the offences of murder, cruel treatment and wanton destruction. And the Chamber found, at paragraph 573, that this displaced all possibility that the conduct occurred by mistake, confusion or accidentally. Tarculovski was present when the crimes occurred. There is no evidence suggesting that he disapproved of the crimes, tried to stop them when they commenced or initiated any sanctions after the -- against the police afterwards. On the contrary, when he appeared before the commission, he did not mention any criminality and refused to reveal the identities of the police. Regarding the preparations, the Trial Chamber found that he was responsible for the preparations for the attack. And that's at paragraphs 555 and 560. On his own admission, Tarculovski confirmed that he personally selected the police reserve volunteers. He was in charge of the timing of the operation. Postponing from the 11th to the 12th. He was involved in procuring the bullet-proof vests, the radio units, the Hermelin that carry -- the Hermelin armoured personnel carrier that carried the gasoline through the village. He secured transportation for the police, and on the day before the attack, he led he reconnaissance mission. Finally, he played a key role in coordinating with the army. He held the planning meeting that you've already have heard of, on 10th of August, to discuss the operation with other senior army and police officials. He arranged for the president to speak with the local army commander to support the operation. He exchanged telephone calls with army officials in relation to the preparation of the attack. And the success of this cooperation is proved by the -- by the fact that the attack again with opening mortar and other fire from the army positions around the village. The events of the attacks, the repetition of the crimes, the careful preparations, and the close cooperation with the army, all provide is support for the Trial Chamber's reasonable conclusion. The Chamber was entitled to conclude that Tarculovski planned the crimes, and that he also ordered and instigated them with either the direct intent or the awareness of the substantial likelihood that these crimes would occur. The appellant has failed to show any error in the Trial Chamber's conclusion. Your Honours, the Trial Chamber's findings in this Judgement were reasonable and were based on the correct law. Grounds 3 to 5 of the appellant's appeal should be dismissed. Unless you have any questions, I would like to hand the podium over to my colleague, Nadia Shihata, to touch briefly on Grounds 6 and 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SHIHATA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Nadia Shihata, and I will present the Prosecution's response to Grounds 6 and 7. With respect to Ground 6, the Chamber was entitled to admit and use statements made by Mr. Tarculovski to a Macedonian commission investigating the events in Ljuboten. As this Chamber is well aware, decisions on the admissibility of evidence fall within the discretion of the Trial Chamber. Here, the Trial Chamber carefully exercised this discretion. It set forth its reasoning in a 25-page decision, correctly identifying and applying the relevant rules and jurisprudence. It found that the statements were relevant, voluntarily made, and bore sufficient indicia of reliability to be admitted. The Defence doesn't dispute any of these findings. Instead, its argument rests entirely on an unsubstantiated policy recommendation that this Chamber adopt a novel exclusionary rule for out of court statements made during national war crimes investigations. This argument is made for the first time on appeal and should therefore be dismissed as waived. But even on its merits, the argument fails. The Defence puts forth nothing to support its assertion that admitting such statements will undermine the Tribunal's Statute or interfere with national investigations. This assertions are speculative, and this very case shows they should not be taken at face value. Here, despite an ongoing ICTY investigation, Mr. Tarculovski appeared before the commission twice and gave his version of what happened. Moreover, ensuring that a Trial Chamber can admit and assess all prima facie relevant and reliable evidence enhances the search for truth and therefore the Tribunal's mission. It does not undermine it. The Defence's appeal in this regard should therefore be dismissed. With respect to the Defence's complaints about the Trial Chamber's use of the statements, we simply note that the Defence's reasoning confuses the prima facie reliability determination that occurs at the admission stage with the finally valuation of evidence. In other respects, I simply refer Your Honours to the arguments we made in our response brief. I will now turn briefly to Ground 7. The Trial Chamber was not required to consider as a mitigating factor Macedonia's grants of amnesty to persons on both sides of the Macedonia NLA conflict. First, the Defence never mentioned amnesty as a mitigating factor in its sentencing arguments at trial. We note that the Appeals Chamber has stated that "an appeal is not the appropriate forum in which mitigating circumstances, evidence of which was readily available at trial, should be presented for the first time." And that's from the Bralo Judgement on sentencing appeal, paragraph 18, and the sources cited therein at footnote 67. We believe that principle should be followed here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you for slowing down.

utterances.speaker: MS. SHIHATA
utterances.text: In addition, the argument assumes, wrongly, that those who committed war crimes, like Mr. Tarculovski, were granted amnesty under Macedonian law. If Your Honours examine the actual language of the Law on amnesty, which was admitted as Exhibit P83, you will see this was not the case. The law specifically excludes those who committed criminal acts under the ICTY's jurisdiction, and further provides that those already convicted of "criminal acts against humanity and international law," are not entitled to amnesty or a reduction in sentence. And I direct Your Honours to Articles 1 and 3 of the law on these points. No one who committed war crimes, like Mr. Tarculovski, or other violations of international humanitarian law was ever granted amnesty. As a result, the Trial Chamber did not abuse its discretion in failing to consider an amnesty never granted to those similarly situated to Mr. Tarculovski. Finally on this mitigation point, we note that a similar amnesty argument was made and rejected in Prosecutor v. Brima, Kamara, and Kamu before the Special Court for Sierra Leone. The Trial Chamber there rejected this argument at paragraphs 137 to 138 of its sentencing Judgement, and this was affirmed on appeal. The Defence also argues in Ground 7 that the Trial Chamber failed to consider Article 40 of the Macedonian Criminal Code which resulted in an incorrect determination of Macedonia's general practice regarding prison sentences. The Trial Chamber committed no discernible error in this regard. First, the Chamber was not bound by Macedonian sentencing practices. It simply had to take them into account. Second, the Trial Chamber didn't consider Article 40 because it was not applicable. Article 40 allows for mitigation of punishment in circumstances where the Court concludes that "especially extenuating circumstances exist." The mitigating factors found by the Chamber here amount to: 1, Mr. Tarculovski's being regarded as a capable and successful officer; 2, his voluntary surrender to the Tribunal; and 3, his proper conduct in detention and during trial. None of these circumstances is exceptional. As a result, there was no reason for the Trial Chamber to refer to Article 40 of the Criminal Code. Ground 7 of Mr. Tarculovski's appeal should therefore be dismissed. And unless Your Honours have any questions, this concludes my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll now have the reply from Mr. Tarculovski's counsel. Yes, Mr. Alan Dershowitz. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution has it exactly backwards when it says that there is no conflict over jus in bellum, but rather the conflict is over jus ad bellum. That's exactly wrong. The conflict over how one deals with terrorism is never about jus ad bellum. That law has now become absolutely clear, Charter Article 51 of the United Nations ^. Of course, you can combat terrorism and take actions. The question is what actions can you take. All of the controversy, all of controversy is about jus in bellum. What are the appropriate rules of engagement when you're fighting terrorism? Can you fire at terrorists who hide behind human shields? Can you destroy houses that were used by terrorists? What are the rules of proportionality? How does one distinguish civilians? The argument that there is it no conflict today, that there are sharp rules that distinguish civilians from combatants, that goes back to the 1900s. Certainly no later than 1940s. Today all of the controversy is who is a civilian and who is a combatant. People who by day wear suicide vests or help people put on suicide vests, and by night they mingle in the population. People who by day plant bombs underneath troop movements, and by night mingle in the population. People who were black a T-shirt without a insignia, people who wear a T-shirt with insignia, people who serve as voluntarily human shields, those are exactly the debates that are going on in academia today. And the very idea that Mr. Tarculovski is supposed to revolve these debates, when all the great academics in the world can't, I was particularly informed by the fact that the opponent cites the Goldstone Report as if it was not controversial. Has there ever been a report more controversial? Now Mr. Goldstone himself recently --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're being asked to slow down. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: Oh, I'm sorry. Judge Goldstone, who you are all familiar with, of course, recently said that one of his criticisms is that Israel should have used commandos. It should have sent commandos into the urban areas, rather than dropping bombs. That's a perfectly plausible argument but that's exactly what was done in this case. So the great dispute is what the rules of engagement, what are the international humanitarian laws when one is dealing with terrorism? These laws were written prior to the advent of the new phenomenon of terrorists who hide behind civilians, who then target civilians, and who then use the civilian deaths as justification for what they are doing to encourage other people to join into their enterprise. That is precisely the conflict, and that conflict has not been resolved. And the mens rea requirement and the requirement of even knowledge of law certainly must take into account the fact that when you have somebody in this intermediate position, he is not supposed to know how to answer those questions. How could he know? The issue that we've raised about jurisdiction, let me be very clear particularly to the question raided by Judge Meron earlier on. We have raised both a macro and a micro challenge to jurisdiction. The macro challenge, which we raise in our brief on paragraph 29, Tarculovski now renews his jurisdictional challenge and notes the fact and that it goes on and on to talk about even if there were to be an armed conflict, and even if the armed conflict were sufficiently intent. The next question is whether or not this particular encounter, if it was within an armed conflict, gives rise to international humanitarian law. Plainly, you can have an armed conflict. It can be intense, and then in the middle of an armed conflict, a bunch of policemen go into a town and rob wallets from people and steal people. That would not give rise to the jurisdiction of this Court. It is not enough to conclude that there is an intense armed conflict, and that was the thrust of much of our brief, but without conceding the intensity of the armed conflict and the macro issue involved in this case. At the very least our argument boils down to this. When you have a case where there is sufficient doubt about the macro, that should be taken into account in deciding the micro. That is, if it is doubtful that there is an intense armed conflict and within that doubtful concept -- context there is an event like this one, in which less than a handful of people who are civilians are killed, there is damage to be sure, but not extensive damage of the kind that is usually associated with the kinds of genocide this court is unfortunately all too familiar with, the question is whether international humanitarian law applies there. And then if it does, what is the international humanitarian law when you're fighting against terrorists, and whether or not the defendant can know these issues. For example, one of the issues raised is, let's assume you have a legitimate battle but you know crimes are going to be committed. The position taken by the Prosecution is you can't sent troops in if you know crimes are being committed, even if you don't intend to do that. That's very controversial. Let's assume, for example, that there are terrorist attacks against civilians in Skopje or any place else, and the only way to respond to is by sending in police and soldiers, knowing that some of the policemen will probably rob. Historically in warfare and police actions policemen rob, soldiers rape. There's looting. There's burning. Does it mean if you know there is going to be some of that, that you can't engage in the battle? No. Rules of proportionality still prevail, and it is not surprising that the Prosecution didn't charge violation of rules of proportionality. Now, there's a lot of context to this as well. For example, in determining jurisdiction this was not the only incident during the Macedonian conflict. There were many terrorist attacks by NLA that killed more civilians than were killed here. But they were not subject to the Court's jurisdiction. The idea of selectively picking one encounter in what was, we submit, not an intense armed struggle but a series of encounters over a short period of time, to pick just one and say that one is subject to international humanitarian law, when others that produced far more casualties and far more civilian casualties, children, women, remember here only men and only men who we believe were reasonably, if wrongly, suspected. Take for example - my brother will deal more with this - the first case of the shooting. You're involved in a situation. The Court finds that there's firing, ongoing firing. You come to the door of a house that you think is harbouring terrorists and a man comes to the door. You don't know who he is and a policeman shoots him. That happens every day in the city of New York. That happens everyday all over the world. Nobody can infer from the shooting of one man at door, when he's trying to close the door or open the door, that that was part of a coordinated plan to kill this individual. Almost premeditated and coordinated. It simply doesn't follow. It may have been a crime --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Dershowitz, can I take you back to a proposition that you set forth earlier. You say, assuming that there is an armed conflict -- MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- at a general level, it meets all the requirements of intensity, et cetera, but in the middle of it, a group of policemen go into a town and rob some wallets. That is on a very small scale. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And your arguments, as I understand it, is that that small scale act would not qualify as an armed conflict, even if it is related -- even if it can be shown to be an integral part of the wider armed conflict. Are you saying that -- MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- small scale act would not qualify? MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: It wouldn't qualify but not for the reason, Mr. President, that you state. Not because it is not part of an armed conflict, because it is not in violation of international humanitarian law. That is, there are two issues that have be decided. One, the issue has to be decided is the conflict in general qualify under the Tadic principles, and I don't have to repeat for the Court the Tadic principles. They're all set out on page 38 of the brief, violation must constitute an infringement of the rule of international humanitarian law. The rule must be customary in nature, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Slow down, please, when reading. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: Oh, I'm sorry. In other words, what we're arguing is that these other requirements are independent, for jurisdictional purposes, of the armed conflict. Our position is there was no intense armed conflict. If you think there was, Your Honour, you still have to decide whether a particular incident involved violation of international humanitarian law. It doesn't follow automatically, just because an incident was part of an armed conflict, that the conduct occurred violated international humanitarian law. If, for example, the rules of engagement were proper, the purpose was proper, but some policemen, in the course of a mixed -- a mixed issue of police and armed activity, violated the law, that doesn't bestow jurisdiction on this Court. And to take your question and put it to Judge Meron's earlier question, yes, if it was a police action, that may impose more obligations to avoid hurting civilians, but that cuts against it being part of an international armed conflict. That is, it points one way for jurisdictional purposes. And what it really says is that if there is a domestic trial of a policeman in a police action, in the domestic trial it may be harder for him to defend himself than it would be for a soldier to defend himself in a military context. In other words, there are greater restrictions on the police, but those restrictions are domestic restrictions. The international restrictions apply to the police and they apply to soldiers. But if the action was done in self-defence and was proportional, et cetera, it doesn't constitute a violation of international humanitarian law just because it happened to be -- it happened to take place while there was an intense armed conflict going on. I hope that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. But the evidence shows that you indiscriminately targeted civilians in that small scale act, that would be in breach of international humanitarian law. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: Well, it would have to show that there was a deliberate wilful plan to target the civilians. If what happened was this, if there was a plan, as we believe there was in this case and as we believe the evidence shows, to go after terrorist and the plan is consistent with going after terrorists, in the course of the plan policemen then do what policemen and what soldiers often do in the fog of war. The idea that that turns what was a proper exercise of authority into an international humanitarian concern is our challenge, and we don't believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: No, I know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: No, we think it is both. And there's a very interesting issue about evidence in doctrine because Your Honours sent the case back to make fact findings as to whether or not there was sufficient intense armed conflict, and the Court applied the wrong standard of proof. We don't think this Court has ever decided the issue. We're aware of it. As to what the standard of proof is on jurisdictional elements of the crime, the Court here did not apply beyond a reasonable doubt standard. It showed reasonable doubt. It virtually admitted there was reasonable doubt, and if I had time, I would go -- I would go into the details of the Court's Judgement as to doubt, but it simply said, We are satisfied, we find. We don't believe that satisfies the jurisdictional requirements of proof beyond a reasonable doubt. We don't believe that the Court was appropriately advised of what the proper standard was. I know, I'm running out of my time, and my brother is pulling at my robe, so I will let him continue. Unless there are any other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You are the best person to encroach on your brother's time. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: And he is the best qualified to complain if I do, so, thank you. MR. N. DERSHOWITZ: My complaining has never worked. Your Honours, Article 25 provides that an Appeals Chamber shall hear appeals from persons convicted by the Trial Chamber or from the Prosecutors on the following grounds: One is an error of law; the second is a error of fact which has occasioned a miscarriage of justice. 98 per cent, maybe 100 per cent, of the presentation that you heard with respect to issues 2, 3 -- 3, 4, and 5, were recitations of conclusions arrived at by the Trial Chamber. And we maintain that if you are going to exercise your power to determine whether there were errors of fact, you have to see whether any of those conclusions that were arrived at had an evidentiary base. Just to repeat what the Trial Court found precludes you from doing your job. And let me give you a number of very specific examples. The Prosecutor mentioned essentially two pieces of evidence that it says supports the notion that Tarculovski was actually leading and present at all of the situations. They make reference to M-037. If you review the testimony of M-037, and if we can go into closed session, I will go over it with Your Honours in detail and show you it is inconceivable for that to be used as a predicate for the conclusion that he was present at each of the sites, and that he was there to commit the crimes on each of the sites. It is such a stretch. Yes, the Trial Chamber found it. Yes, the Trial Chamber went out of its way to say, We rely upon M-037. But if you read those pages that are referred to, it does not support the conclusion. And I am suggesting to this Chamber that it has an obligation to exercise Section B to review that. Just because they say it, doesn't mean it's so. Just because the Chamber says it, doesn't mean it's so. The evidence is not there. Second, they say that the statement that was made by Tarculovski supports it. His presence in the town, in the village, does not support the conclusion that he was present at the Jusufi shooting, that he was present at the Ametovski house when the shooting took place, that he was present when they don't even know where he was, where anybody was when the third person was shot. So, yes, it is in there. Yes, it says so. Yes, it is wrong, as a matter of law. With respect to the actus reus, for the first time now, my adversary is suggesting that the Trial Chamber erred in describing the requirements for actus reus. They never raised that before. They've never noted any problem. And with the language, they're citing a number of court decisions says -- is that you'd need at both the preparatory and execution phase. So the trial proceeded on that basis. To now say the Trial Court was wrong and the findings were wrong and a law was wrong in that situation, I suggest that it's inappropriate to be raised at the present time. There was a requirement as articulated by the Trial Court relying upon Trial Court determinations, all of which said that you need both preparatory stage and the execution stage. If you now find as a matter of law that that is the requirement, and I'm reading from paragraph -- they refer -- it's paragraph -- sorry, I don't have the cite. But the citation is to footnotes in paragraph 572, and it describes what the actus reus is. This Court then has to make a determination as to whether the Trial Court's determination was correct without an objection having been raised as to what the Trial Court said. With regard to the mens rea, it is only in the context of mens rea, is substantial likelihood enter the picture. And there you can say he either committed it or there's a substantial likelihood that the crime was committed. Let me deal with that last claim for a second. There are three references in that whole Judgement to the substantial likelihood that a crime can be committed. Two of them are in definitional sections of the mens rea, and the last one is a tag-on sentence at the end of the Judgement which says: "Alternatively, we can conclude that there was a substantial likelihood that he knew." Nonetheless, there is not an analysis of that, no description of it, and to the extent there is a suggestion that he was not experienced, how do you draw the inference that he had an awareness that the substantial likelihood that the crime would be committed in the execution of the plan? His lack of knowledge, his lack of experience all suggest to the contrary, and if there is any reliance upon that mens rea provision, I suggest there was an obligation of the Trial Chamber to analyse it. It's an obligation to have a reasoned decision. You can't simply say, pronounce, that he had, in its final sentence, a substantial awareness without doing any analysis. But I must come back to the major thrust of what I am suggesting, and that is if you summarise, as the Prosecutor did, all of the conclusions made by the Trial Court and never examined the substance, why, what evidence, what basis, then I believe that there is a serious problem. Let just touch on one final point. The Prosecutor emphasised that the Trial Court, just as an example, said that Jusufi was shot at close range. There's a citation to the autopsy. There is nothing in the autopsy, nothing in the autopsy that says that Jusufi was shot at close range. So Jusufi could have been shot from the hill overlooking, by the military. But they argue, and the Trial Court finds, close range was important because the police were close. But if there is no support for the notion, close range was just made up, then it is an error of fact which is a material error of fact. They have told you it is a material factor for which there is no basis in the records. So I suggest, yes, it says close range. Yes, the Prosecutor says close range. Yes, shots were fired. But whether the shot that killed Jusufi was at close range, zero evidence to support that notion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll take the break now, one hour. We'll resume at 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.56 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So Mr. Rogers, and in relation to Boskoski.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. Your Honours, I address the Prosecution appeal against the acquittal of Ljube Boskoski on all counts. And I shall address three main areas in my submission to you this afternoon. The first is the notion and principle behind the doctrine of command responsibility and the current legal position under this doctrine, as far as it can be ascertained. Secondly, the issue of reporting and its sufficiency or otherwise as a measure capable of discharging the legal duty imposed under Article 7(3), and in that context I will attempt to answer Your Honours' question. And finally, I shall then address the application of the principle to the facts as found. But, Your Honours, let me first summarise the Prosecution appeal by way of introduction in this way. Paragraph 16 of the Hadzihasanovic interlocutory appeal decision on command responsible the Appeals Chamber held: "Command responsibility is the most effective method by which international criminal law can enforce responsible command." Instilling the principles of responsible command in a superior is one method to ensure that their subordinates respect the legal principles governing armed conflict. The ICRC's empirical research, "The Roots of Behaviour in War," looked at the most effective means of preventing international humanitarian law violations. After surveying some 15.000 civilians and combatants in 15 war zones and reviewing the available literature, the ICRC concluded at page 16 that: "The main thing is not to persuade combatants that they must behave in a different way, or to win them over personally, but to influence the people who have ascendency over them ..." In the context of an armed conflict, where the rules of international humanitarian law apply, those in authority over subordinates are required to exercise that authority responsibly. Responsible command requires superiors to act responsibly, and it is our submission that Ljube Boskoski did not. The Chamber found that he possessed alarming information about crimes, including unlawful killing, Judgement 527. And certainly by latest 5th September 2001, he knew of the serious allegations against the police in Ljuboten on the 12th of August, and in the days following. Trial Judgement 451. This covered the police station crimes, as well as the destruction, cruel treatment, and murder allegations arising from the attack on the village itself. And, Your Honours, it is important to remember that there are two groups of crimes. There is the Ljuboten itself crimes, if you like, and then the police station crimes. Boskoski took no, in our submission, genuine positive action to have the crimes of his subordinates punished. None of the reports he received made any mention of crimes by police, either in Ljuboten, or in relation to any of the victims of cruel treatment, at Buzalak check-point, Butel police station, Prolece police station, Bit Pazar police station, or Karpos police station. No crimes by police were ever reported to the competent authorities. His public statements about the Ljuboten incidents indicate he that he had no intention, we say, of ensuring police crime -- police crime was investigated. In his book, Exhibit P402, where he writes of these events, relating -- referring to the OSCE investigation into Ljuboten, he accused the OSCE, who visited on the 14th of August, of trial trying to "misinform the public that allegedly the Macedonian security forces in the clashes did not kill five terrorists but citizens of Ljuboten." He dismissed out of hand such allegations, that is, allegations of the murder of citizens by security forces as "the most striking slander about the security forces." The allegations that he had received from the OSCE were reinforced by a Human Rights Watch investigation and report. Responding to the allegations of the crimes in relation to that report, and those are crimes alleged by police, of course, in the media he said: "I will press charges for the Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg," because the Human Rights Watch claims "undermine," as he said, "not only the dignity of the Macedonian Ministry of Interior but also my personal dignity." Trial Judgement 450, Exhibit P359. Your Honours, in the references that he made in the interviews that he gave, not any time did he say anything like, in the exhibits that are before the Court, I am taking these responsibilities very seriously; we are investigating the allegations of crimes against the police, and we will ensure that all is done to identify that. Your Honours may feel that is something might -- he might be expected to have said at the time. Your Honour, the error in this case is that the Trial Chamber erred when it failed to convict him for his failure to punish the criminal conduct of his subordinates arising from the attack on Ljuboten of the 12th of August. It took too narrow a view of what Ljube Boskoski could and should have done to address this criminal offending by his subordinates. It took this view because it applied a wrong legal test concerning what is expected of a commander under Article 7(3) of the Statute to punish the crimes of his subordinates. It focussed solely on the sufficiency of any reporting in the sense as to whether it was likely to trigger an investigation into the crimes, rather than what steps were within the material possibility of Ljube Boskoski's power to take to punish his subordinates. In short, it ignored the totality of what he could have done and looked only at the reporting measure. In considering the reports as a sufficient measure, it ignored as a fact the other measures open to him, and that the reports themselves were not sufficient to address the criminal conduct, all of the criminal conduct, of his subordinates in a way that would meet the requirement to take the necessary and reasonable measures. These are aspects of the same factual error; namely, that the reports, as were made, were insufficient to satisfy his obligation under Article 7(3) to punish. To amplify a little more the principle underlying superior responsibility, the principle of responsible command lies at the heart of Article 7(3). It is a concept that expresses the manner in which a superior in a position of authority is expected to exercise the powers inherent in that position. In an armed conflict, that authority must be exercised with full respect for applicable international humanitarian law norms. The superior, for example, has a duty to ensure civilians are not targeted unlawful, that prisoners are accorded proper treatment, et cetera. When those subordinated to the superior act outside of those norms, and in order to ensure conformity with them by those subordinates and others, he has an additional duty to ensure they are punished. That, of course, is reflected in the frame of the Statute under Article 7(3). As the Appeals Chamber expressed in the Hadzihasanovic interlocutory appeals decision at paragraph 22: "The elements of command responsibility are derived from the elements of responsible command." And that: "The concept of responsible command looks to the duties comprised in the idea of command." In developing the legal parameters of command responsibility, the Appeals Chamber has sought not to unfairly impose an absolute burden on the superior for the criminal conduct of his subordinates. It has first required proof that he is in a position of authority over them, that they are actually subordinates. And, to that end, it has addressed and developed the concept of effective control. In this case, the Trial Chamber addressed this at Trial Judgement 513, 514, 515, and 516. It has then required the superior to have knowledge or reason to know, inquiry notice of the criminal conduct. In this case, the Trial Chamber addressed this at Trial Judgement paragraph 527 and 536. And it is elaborated a little more in our appeal brief at paragraph 60 to 61. Finally, and importantly, it has required that the superior must take the well-known phrase "necessary and reasonable measures" to prevent the crimes or punish the perpetrator thereof. Comes from the Halilovic Appeals Judgement, paragraph 59. Going on to explain what it meant, at Judgement paragraph 63 in the same case, the Appeals Chamber defined the necessary and reasonable measures, as far as it was able, in this ways: "Necessary measures are the measures appropriate for the superior to discharge his obligation (showing that he genuinely tried to prevent or punish) and reasonable measures are those reasonably falling within the material powers of the superior." It may be suggested this to some extent it is a little circular. But what is clear is that it is a broad test. It is not narrow. And it is not restrictive. But it is clear that the steps taken must be genuine. They must be real, they must be true. The obligation to prevent criminal conduct or to punish is, we submit, an active, not a passive duty. It requires affirmative action by a superior to take steps to control those subordinated to him. Quote comes from the US v. Karl Brandt. I see Mr. Mettraux smiles, as he is very familiar with these provisions. Referred to in the Halilovic Appeals Judgement at paragraph 63, footnote 167. In the Strugar Trial Judgement, at paragraph 376, the Trial Chamber noted this: "Military Tribunals established after World War II have interpreted the superior's duty to punish as implying an obligation for the superiors to conduct an effective investigation" - I refer to Yamashita, footnote 1099 - "and to take active steps to secure that the perpetrators will be brought to justice." High Command, footnote 1100. "Relevant in this respect," they said, "could also be whether the superior has called for a report on the incident and the thoroughness of the investigation." And they refer to Tojo, footnote 1101, where the IMT convicted Tojo for not taking adequate steps to "punish the offenders and prevent the commission of similar offences in the future ... he did not call for a report into the incident ... made perfunctory inquiries about the march but took no action. No one was punished." It is an affirmative duty, Your Honours, because unruly subordinates are a dangerous entity. As the Appeals Chamber recognised in Hadzihasanovic Appeals Judgement at paragraph 30, a superior's failure to punish a crime: "Is likely to be understood by his subordinates at least as acceptance if not encouragement, of such conduct with the effect of increasing the risk of new crimes being committed." This is why he must act. Even the Trial Chamber accepted that Boskoski must take active steps to ensure that the offenders are punished. Trial Judgement 519. This is why he must take all the necessary and reasonable measures within his material possibility to punish. The duty cannot be abrogated. This affirmative duty requires a superior to do all in his power, we submit, to ensure subordinates are punished. This is supported by the Trial Chamber's approach to the assessment of guilt in the Aleksovski case, Trial Judgement 117, where they considered Aleksovski's responsibility in this way: "Despite the authority he had, the accused took no measures to prevent the crimes committed. Nor did the accused use everything in his power to attempt to punish the guards responsible for them." This approach was not disapproved by the Appeals Chamber when it considered the accused's appeal against his conviction under Article 7(3), and when it dismissed his appeal against conviction for failing to punish the guards at the prison for their criminal conduct. Interestingly, on the facts of the Aleksovski case, the Trial Chamber found: "None of the reports transmitted to the military police commander or to the president of the Travnik military tribunal dealt with the assaults committed by guards or HVO soldiers within Kaonik prison." It's this case upon which the respondent and the Chamber relied to suggest that "civilian superiors, who may lack the disciplinary or sanctioning powers of military commanders, may discharge their obligation to punish by reporting to the competent authorities whenever a crime has been committed, if these reports are likely to trigger an investigation or initiate disciplinary or criminal proceedings." That's Trial Judgement 418 and 519. But the Aleksovski Trial Judgement, Your Honours, at paragraph 78, in which that principle is said to be derived, was not addressing the question of necessary and reasonable measures, but whether the accused had de facto or de jure authority over the guards, and the ability to report in a manner likely to trigger an investigation is relevant to that consideration. Where the accused is a civilian superior, it is his position in the hierarchy which would influence their likely punishment and thus help to establish the relationship of effective control. In fact, the reports in the Aleksovski case did not mention the crimes of Aleksovski's subordinates. In that case, it was found they were the military police guards. And he was convicted. The Trial Chamber was not considering the question of measures in Trial Judgement paragraph 78 in Aleksovski. Your Honours, the notion of doing all within your power is developed in the Hadzihasanovic Trial Judgement at paragraph 1061, we say. Hadzihasanovic was acquitted, because once the matter was referred there to the investigating judge, he was "unable to carry out his own criminal investigations or to influence how the cases with dealt with by Judge Mirsad Strika or the competent prosecutor." He couldn't do any more. In this case, the police retained the ability to continue to investigate at the pre-criminal stage, at Article 142 of the Code, Exhibit P88, Code of Criminal Procedure in Macedonia. Even if they had no absolute duty to do so, they retained the power. And, Your Honours, I also direct to you footnote 1982 in the Trial Judgement, where this notion of what they could do was further developed. They could have submitted additional reports relating to the crimes of subordinates. There was more Boskoski could have done, unlike in the Hadzihasanovic case. To be sure, and to ensure the risk of further crimes is reduced, the measures taken must be immediate and they must be visible. This requires affirmative action. In the Hadzihasanovic Appeals Judgement, at paragraph 152, the Appeals Chamber said this: "Indeed, while immediate and visible measures, such as disciplinary detention were necessary, the disciplinary sanction of a period of detention not exceeding 60 days" was insufficient, on the facts of that case. The point being that even the Hadzihasanovic Appeals Chamber recognised that visible and immediate measures were needed, even if, on the facts, the measure taken wouldn't have been enough to suffice. More was needed on top of what had already been done. Turning to the question of reporting. Much in this case, of course, has focussed on this issue of reporting. We reiterate that this is but one measure that may suffice, but it must be considered along with the other measures open to the superior that were within his material possibility. This is a broad, not a narrow, test. Reporting will not automatically satisfy the duty to punish. As the Appeals Chamber in Hadzihasanovic, at 154, said: "A superior need not dispense punishment personally and may discharge his duty to punish by reporting the matter to the competent authorities." May discharge. Possibly. This, in turn, cites the Blaskic Trial Judgement approved in the Appeals Judgement in Blaskic which says: "The measure of submitting reports is again an example applicable 'under some circumstances.'" "What constitutes such measures is not a matter of substantive law but of evidence." And that, Your Honours, goes a little way to answer Your Honours' question. In Blaskic Appeals Judgement 417, the Appeals Chamber endorses this approach. When approving the Celebici Trial Chamber they said: "We conclude that a superior should be held respond for failing to take such measures as are within his material possibility." And in Halilovic Appeals Judgement 182, the Appeals Chamber again said: "As the Trial Chamber correctly outlined, the duty to punish includes at least an obligation to investigate possible crimes or have the matter investigated to establish the facts, and if the superior has no power to sanction, to report them to the competent authorities." In other words, what it is possible for him to have done, he should have done. This, of course, presupposes an investigation prior to a report, and then a report which will lead to sanction when he has no power to sanction. The responsibility for sanction is not moved on, but, rather, on the facts of a given case, an investigation followed by a report may be enough to discharge. Despite referring to these very cases at paragraph 17 of his respondent's brief and despite their clear language, the respondent boldly asserts that: "The Appeals Chamber has made it clear that reporting to the competent authorities would satisfy the superior's duty to punish whenever the accused does not have the power himself to sanction crimes of subordinates." The implication of this bold statement is that only a report is required, and this acts as a form of guillotine to responsibility. This is a theme which is developed in the brief by suggesting that reporting removes the superior's responsibility for punishment onto others. That's found in his brief at paragraph 27. And, further, that the ICTY jurisprudence supports this proposition. He cites the Halilovic at 182, Appeals Judgement. Unfortunately, we say, for the respondent, none of the appeals cases he cites to support that proposition at all. What is the matter that must be reported? Well, it's obvious. The matter that must be reported are the suspected crimes of the subordinates, and it is these that must be punished. Anything less than this will not suffice to discharge the command responsibility arising from the position of responsibility as a superior. In the Oric Appeals Judgement at paragraph 59, the Appeals Chamber stressed that: "Knowledge of a crime and knowledge of a person's criminal conduct are, in law and in fact, distinct matters." The relevance is this: Mere knowledge of a crime will not engage a duty to punish because it is not connected to the subordinate for whom the superior is responsible. Hence, it is knowledge of a subordinate's criminal conduct, or reason to know, that engages the potential responsibility, and thus, it is, that this is what must be punished. Or in the context of reporting, if that is the measure, it is that which must be reported. In this case, the Trial Chamber found as follows, Trial Judgement 536: "There was sufficient information available to him that the police may have committed crimes. As their superior, Ljube Boskoski was obliged to report this to the competent authorities." Yet, Your Honours, the reports in this case did not allege that crimes had been committed, we say, nor that they had been committed by Ljube Boskoski's subordinates. And in particular, they never mentioned the police station crimes, for which he was also charged, whatever they may have said about deaths in the village. The respondent misapplies the separate Strugar opinions in his brief at paragraph 29, we say, to suggest that whenever an independent authority is looking into an incident, the duty to punish is displaced. In fact, and some of Your Honours will recall, I'm sure, the opinions, they relate to the principle of singleness of command within the JNA. A superior, who also has his own 7(3) responsibility, within the same chain of command as the accused, thus not an independent authority, takes over or institutes an investigation into the conduct of subordinates who are the subordinates of both the accused and the superior instituting the investigation. Because the accused is himself the subordinate of the superior taking over, and the offending subordinates are both of their subordinates, the notion of one single command displaces the accused. His function is taken over by another within the same command. In this case, there is no higher command, as in Strugar, only a parallel organisation, which does itself does not have any 7(3) responsibility, and to which the report is made.
