Only if a sufficiently detailed and proper report is made that addresses the offending of subordinates might it be sufficient to discharge the criminal responsibility under Article 7(3), and then, only after considering what other measures were possible for him to take to show that he genuinely tried to do all he could to punish. In this case, the Ministry of Interior were able to continue to investigate under Article 142 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. That is, they could carry out inquiries. So there is a trap in the term "investigate." I don't use "investigate" in the sense of the investigating judge's investigation; I use it in the sense of carrying out an inquiry into whether a crime has been committed. The general broad sense as we all understand what an investigation is, not in the technical sense that may be used under the Code of Criminal Procedure. And you can continue -- they can continue to investigate despite reports to the judicial authorities, and the respondent accepts that's the case in his brief, at paragraph 115. Although he says they were not obliged to do such things but they were able to garner such information. It sounds like an investigation to me. In this case, Your Honours, the crimes of Boskoski's subordinates were never investigated. He argues that under Macedonian law it was practice to report an incident. And that's in his brief at 216. And to suggest that there's a report into a broad general incident where several crimes are believed to have been committed. Notification is given once and once only in relation to the entire incident, and refers to a number of citations in his footnote at 365. But, Your Honours, in our submission, a proper analysis of those citations show they do not support that proposition. The statement relied upon comes from a report of the witness Taseva, which is Exhibit 1D310, paragraph 85. But that report in turn cites the evidence of Witness Ruskovska at transcript 1541 to 2, and Witness Toskovski at transcript 4373 to 4. And it is clear from reading this evidence that the witnesses were referring to the fact that an investigating judge may expand the nature of an investigation, used in the technical sense of the investigation. That is at a stage later to reporting, and is not the same as a once and for all general notification. Indeed, Witness Ruskovska refers to the judge being able to ask the prosecutor to expand the investigation, in her words, into one more crime or perpetrator. Transcript 1542. In addition, the witness Taseva, upon whom they rely, refers to Articles 557 to 8 of the code for this notion of a general incident report, but those Articles of the code arise at the investigation stage and are the powers by which the investigating judge can expand the investigation. In any event, Article 158 of the Macedonian Criminal Code is clear: "The investigation is only in reference of that crime or against that accused to whom the decision on conducting investigation refers." Exhibit P88. Your Honours, turning to the question of delegation, as a general principle, Your Honours, we say that -- there is -- Boskoski says that there was no power to report crimes because he was not competent to do so. And that's in his brief at 164 to 167. First of all, the Trial Chamber did not find that he knew crimes had been reported, but, rather, that he knew a report had been made notifying the judiciary of deaths. Trial Judgement 529. It went on to find that, if followed up correctly, this would, in its opinion, have likely led to the discovery of the crimes. That's also at 529. The question of his competency to act, that is to report absent an express power to do so, was roundly rejected by the Trial Chamber as a misunderstanding of the relevant legislation. That's 507 and 510 of the Trial Judgement. And in particular the Trial Chamber noted that the minister had the duty to ensure the work of his ministry is performed lawfully and efficiently, and that this requires the minister be able to order and determine the work to be performed, and to enforce compliance. At Trial Judgement 513 and 516, they found that he had de jure and de facto authority to ensure the criminal police of the MOI performed their functions efficiently and lawfully, and that he had and could effectively exercise the required command responsibility. Boskoski seeks to argue that he can delegate this responsibility and then assume competent execution absent material to notify him otherwise. He says that this is matter of international law, in his brief at 170 to 176, and refers to the High Command case. But in our submission the contextual analysis of this Judgement shows that the issue being decided was different. The issue for von Leeb was whether he had knowledge of unlawful activity, as the court was concerned not to convict him merely because subordinates had committed crimes. The issue was not whether, knowing of crimes himself, he was entitled to rely upon subordinate to discharge a function to report crimes. Where he did know of unlawful orders and the commission of crimes, the Tribunal considered what it was he did to deal with it, and where they considered his actions were insufficient they convicted him, for example in relation to the implementation of the Barbarossa jurisdiction order. Your Honours asked the question: "As a question of law, is it possible for a superior to satisfy his duty under Article 7(3) of the Statute if he effectively takes no necessary or reasonable measures to punish his subordinates because he is informed" --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. I'll just go back to the question. I'm sure Your Honours are familiar with it. "As a question of law, is it possible for a superior to satisfy his duty under Article 7(3) if he effectively takes no necessary or reasonable measures to punish his subordinates because he is informed that his subordinates have taken certain steps which may result in their punishment?" Our answer, no. To the extent of the superior's material possibility, the accused must ensure that the perpetrators will be punished. The measures he needs to take are those reasonably falling within his material powers. That is, what he is reasonably able to do to punish. What the necessary and reasonable measures are will depend on the facts, where he relies on subordinates to take some or all of them. At the very at least, the superior must follow up to determine what steps have been taken and whether they there are any other steps reasonably falling within his powers, that is, are reasonably available to them, to take to ensure that the criminal conduct is punished as far as he can. This necessarily implies some affirmative action on his part, and will be positive conduct capable of amounting to necessary and reasonable measures. On the facts there may be other measures he also needs to take. Your Honours, I'm conscious the answer I have given is somewhat circular. That may be because the jurisprudence available has a certain degree of circularity within it, in any event, but I hope that it goes somewhere to assist. An illustration, Your Honours, of our approach and why we say that is the correct answer is found in the Aleksovski Trial Judgement. I will take you back to the quote I gave to you earlier. Where applying what it understood to be the relevant law, the Trial Chamber stated that the accused did not: "Use everything in his power to attempt to punish the guards responsible." Perhaps that more appropriately summarises what I'm trying to say. The finding was not criticised on appeal as an incorrect assessment of what it was he was required to do. Indeed, the Appeals Chamber noted in Aleksovski without any criticism that the appellant had agreed with the Trial Chamber that he an obligation to "take all the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent or punish the perpetrators." The Appeals Chamber's approach in Blaskic is consistent with this, when it approved the Celebici test, that the superior should be responsible: "For failing to take such measures as are within his material possibility." That approach is consistent with the duty under Article 86 of Additional Protocol I, with the notion of responsible command and with the genuine attempt being made to punish. Turning to this case, Boskoski had the power to control and direct the police - Trial Judgement 513 - which included ensuring the police responsible for investigating what had occurred performed their functions sufficiently and lawfully. He was a man whose strength of personality and energy led him to enjoy success in influencing and guiding the personnel of his ministry and in securing - and that's the way the Trial Chamber put it - their deferment to his proposals. He gained a sense of loyalty and cooperation throughout all levels of the ministry. Trial Judgement 516. He knew of the allegations that crimes had been committed. And this quickly came to his attention. Trial Judgement 527 and 536. On the 12th of August, he was present on the outskirts of Ljuboten for well over an hour. He saw the burning houses and heard the firing. He saw persons detained at Brace's house. Trial Judgement 523. He was interviewed incidentally for television at Brace's house the same day. Trial Judgement 525. Point being, Your Honours, that he was clearly involved in what was going on. There's no finding that he saw any of the crimes. The Trial Chamber veered away from that. But the point is he was there. He was active. He was involved. He had a position of authority within the ministry. He was influential in what was going on. He possessed alarming information about crimes, including unlawful killing. Trial Judgement 527. And as I have already recorded earlier, by the 5th of September, latest, he knew of the serious allegations relating to both the 12th of August and the police stations. Trial Judgement 451. Responding to those allegations in the media, he said he would press charges against the Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg because the claims undermined his dignity and that of the ministry. He received four reports between the 14th and the 17th of August, 2001, 1D361, 364, 373, and 374. Recorded in the Judgement at 447. These related specifically to the Ljuboten events and specifically addressed the actions and investigations being undertaken. None of them mentioned any crimes of subordinates. In his book, writing about the matters that he records he says this. This is Exhibit P402, referring to these incidents: "In the communique of the Ministry of Internal Affairs we had to emphasise that representatives of the OSCE who managed to enter the village tried to misinform the public that allegedly the Macedonian security forces in the clashes did not kill five terrorists but citizens of Ljuboten." He goes on to state that the Ministry of Interior condemned the spreads of misinformation by the OSCE and the most striking slander about the security forces of the Republic of Macedonia. His interviews given at the time confirm his hostility to the allegations of criminal activity by the police. For example, Exhibit P362, a transcript of a television interview he gave on the 14th of August, he said: "The residents of the village of Ljuboten buried those five terrorists. All that remains now is to establish whether they were from Ljuboten itself or whether terrorists were also imported. And this was most probably done with the aim of concealing the traces of the crime they committed. In order to discover the truth, the Prosecutor will need authorisation to perform exhumation in accordance with legal procedure if we want the truth to be confirmed." But in our submission, the truth that he was seeking to confirm was not whether the police had committed any crimes, but whether the terrorists had come from outside of Ljuboten. As the Trial Chamber found, Judgement 535, there was more he could have done to inform himself and ensure the police performed their duties so that the public prosecutor and the investigative judge were in a better position to determine what really had occurred and whether criminal charges against any of the police were justified. But they found that the evidence suggested he was not motivated in that way. It's fact that they could continue to investigate is consistent with the pre-criminal phase of the investigation and Article 142 of the Code. That enables the ministry to undertake the necessary measures to find the perpetrators of crime, collect evidence and reports for use in the "successful conduct of criminal proceedings." Even the respondent agrees that they could do this. Indeed, at the same time as police crimes should have been investigated, the police were able to and did investigate the alleged crimes of the terrorists, so-called. They filed detailed criminal reports against them, specifying perpetrators and specific crimes; P31. They undertook paraffin glove tests of the alleged terrorists, submitted additional reports of their findings. And indeed, the additional report on Atulla Qaili, upon which the Trial Chamber relied to show that his death had been reported, was a report made in connection with an investigation against him and not in relation to an investigation concerning police crimes. As minister in charge of the ministry, having the knowledge of a range of alleged crimes, having received a range of reports, none of which indicated crimes of any subordinates had been reported, he cannot have discharged his duty to punish. In particular in relation to the police station crimes, no reports about these were ever made. They cannot reasonably have been considered as part of the events in Ljuboten. They are separate and distinct crimes. The report relating to Atulla Qaili, for example, only reported his death and not the cause. It made no mention of his mistreatment at the police station, or before. No mention was ever made of criminal conduct of police in relation to the other victims at the police stations or the Buzalak check-point. There was seven victims at Buzalak, one at Butel, seven in Prolece, five in Bit Pazar, and two in Karpos. I accept that there may have been a degree of overlap with some of these because they were moved from one to the other and beaten in each. But nevertheless, a separate crime occurs in each location, none of which are reported to the investigating judge or the public prosecutor. He had the power to assist in this investigation and direct the police to cooperate. Article 142 permitted further investigative activities despite judicial involvement. He had disciplinary measures which were open to him. He could have sought information as to how the investigation into these crimes were ongoing, in order to ensure, as far as he could, that they were punished. No normal police investigations were ever carried out. Indeed, the Trial Chamber found, at 547 in its Judgement, that the police inactivity evidenced: "A serious and scandalous attempt to protect the men involved and represents a grave failure to carry out their responsibilities at the level of OVR Cair." One which would appear to have been countenanced by more senior police. Your Honours, I accept that the Chamber found that -- that the accused had no -- they found had no reason to know that things were not being done properly. But this is what was actually going on and what they found about what was actually going on at the time. Your Honours, the interview he gave on the 14th of August, 2001, P362, and the other statements he made at the time, reveal his understanding of the purpose of any investigation, which was to establish the truth about whether terrorists were local or imported. Indeed as cited in the Judgement, deputy public prosecutor Dragoljub Cakic stated that: "Our objective was not to clarify what happened at Ljuboten. Our objective was only to carry out an exhumation and to identify the persons buried in the local cemetery in the village of Ljuboten." Trial Judgement 456. International humanitarian law imposed an obligation on Ljube Boskoski to ensure the crimes of his subordinates were punished. He had the power to investigate, to have them investigated to provide information to the competent authorities, to ensure a proper report was compiled, to supervise, to discipline. He could have supervised better. Trial Judgement 535. Despite this obligation, he did nothing. And for doing nothing, he was acquitted. Your Honours, we invite you to overturn the acquittal and to substitute convictions in relation to the crimes for which he was charged. Your Honours, those are my submissions. Unless I can assist you, in answer to any questions I will pause and return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Judge Liu has a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Rogers, especially for answering the questions we posed to you concerning the Article 7(3), the command responsibility. In practice in certain situations in a structure like a ministry, for instance, the Ministry of Interior or Justice, the minister himself is impossible to involve, personally involved in every investigation ever, you know, fact-finding mission himself. He may delegate his power to investigate to his police, to his subordinates, to do that. And in this particular case, the Defence may claim that, you know, he was in -- mistaken of the facts, that the matter has been taken care of, that his subordinate. So my question to you is that, you know, do you think the -- the head of the ministry while delegating his power of investigation to his subordinate, also shifts or delegates his command responsibility to his subordinate? The second question is more specific. That is, do you have any evidence to show that Mr. Boskoski knew that the police failed to perform their duty, delegated by him, to investigate this matter? And -- and does he know that reports was not fully or not accurate or not, you know, detailed, you know, concerning of those incidents? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, obviously a number of matters there, a compound question. Let me try to break it down. In relation to the question as to whether he can delegate his command responsibility to his subordinates, the answer is clearly no. He cannot delegate his command responsibility. He retains the responsibility. It ask a personal, we say, obligation upon him. And I have to set out at some length, and that's why I did it, the historical root of this notion. He can't just delegate it away. He has to ensure that it is performed efficiently and properly. And even if he could invite someone to carry out an investigation, there must remain an obligation upon him to ensure that that investigation has been carried efficiently and properly, and that the appropriate information is passed on and acted upon, because the obligation is upon him to take the necessary and reasonable measures to punish, to punish, to ensure punishment occurs. And Your Honours, of course, in relation to international humanitarian law violations we're not talking about a theft of a bag of sweets, which it may not be necessary for him to follow up. We're talking here about grave violations of international humanitarian law and a principle that -- that involves his personal responsibility for the crimes of his subordinates. It is not the same as an obligation or as obligations that might arise under ordinary domestic law, where anybody has an obligation to report or to let police investigate crimes, for example. This is a different form of obligation, and part of the difficulty in this case is that the two notions coincide and can be a little confusing, because of the particular functions within the Ministry of Interior. But he retains command responsibility, and it is that command responsibility which engages his criminal responsibility. And it is through that criminal responsibility that international humanitarian law is enforced, international criminal law is enforced. That is why he can't just delegate it away. As to your question whether there is evidence that he knew police had failed to perform. Your Honours, there is. The reports that he received, which the Trial Chamber found he had received, the four reports, the 1D363. I can't remember them now, but there are four of them. I listed them earlier. Those four reports form the basis of the knowledge that the Trial Chamber found he had concerning the reporting of the incidents. Those four reports make no reference at all to crimes of subordinates being investigated. Therefore, he cannot have had knowledge that the crimes of the subordinates were being investigated. And so he could not have been satisfied that his duty was discharged. Those are my answers to Your Honours' questions. 1D361, 364, 373, and 374. They are referred to in the Trial Judgement. I can give you the reference. 447. But I have to take you back to 529 where they're picked up in footnote 1976, two of them are picked in 1976, and also Exhibit P402 which is his book. And the other reports that the Chamber found he had between the relevant period are found in 447. So the information about what had happened is in those reports and is clear from those reports that crimes have not been reported, in our submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Just a follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think you said that the Trial Chamber found that there was sufficient information available to him that the police may have committed crimes --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- is the finding of the trial judgements, I believe. And I wonder whether this includes the incidents happened in the police station or not, as you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it does. It does cover the incidents in the police station because those were referred to within the Human Rights Watch report of which the Chamber found he had knowledge. And I'm not sure about the OSCE part, but certainly the Human Rights Watch report. I'll check that and make sure whether there is anything else I can tell you. But certainly it comes from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rogers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the Scheduling Order was suggesting we would have a break, but I'm ready to start, if that's Your Honours' wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll break for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Mettraux, you're up next.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Mr. President. Guenael Mettraux appearing on behalf of Ljube Boskoski. I will commence, Your Honour, our presentation with discussing a number of legal issues which arise from this appeal, in particular, in relation to the question that Your Honour Judge Robinson addressed to the party last week. We have [indiscernible] question as a request for assistance to determine what the law on that point is and not as the appellant appears to have treated it, as a partisan rendition of what the law ought to be. In response and in short, Your Honour, the answer to your question is a qualified yes. The manner in which, as a matter of international law, a superior can fulfil his duty to punish depends on the circumstances. Where the superior has the power to punish or sanction subordinates, he can take steps himself to see the punishment of the subordinates, or he can delegate that responsibility to subordinates or others. This is the case, Your Honour, that was relevant to Mr. Aleksovski, the case that the Prosecution has been citing this afternoon. Where, however, he possesses no such power and authority, customary international law provides that he can fulfil his duty to punish by having the matter remitted to the competent authorities for that purpose. I will discuss later today, Your Honours, a number of authorities, which we have cited in tab 1 of the binder that we have distributed, and which establish that under international law such a course of action is both legitimate and sufficient to fulfil a superior's duty to punish whenever the superior does not himself possess the power to sanction. An expression or an illustration of that position, Your Honours, may be found, for instance, in paragraph 420 and 422 of the recent Bemba Confirmation of Charges decision of the ICC which, I should underline, relies solely upon Judgement and authorities from the ICTY. This is what the Court said: "The duty to punish requiring the superior to take the necessary measure to sanction the commission of crimes may be fulfilled in two different ways. Either by the superior himself, taking the necessary and reasonable measures to punish his forces, or, if he does not have the ability to do so, by referring the matter to the competent authorities." And at paragraph 422 the ICC continued about the duty to submit the matter to the competent authorities by saying this: "This duty to submit the matter to the competent authorities remedies the situation where commanders do not have the ability to sanction their forces." It is relevant in that regard to note that the Trial Chamber, at paragraph 519 and 418, among others, did find that Mr. Boskoski had no personal power to punish subordinates for the underlying crimes and the Prosecution did not appeal these findings, neither did it make that allegation at trial. Mr. Boskoski was therefore entitled, as a matter of international law, to fulfil his duty to punish by having the matter reported to the competent authorities, as happened in this case. In that sense, the remittal of the case to the competent authority may be said to constitute necessary and reasonable measure for the purpose of a superior duty, as was noted at paragraph 632 of the Blaskic Appeals Chamber Judgement, which is at tab 1 of your binder. It is well established under customary international law that the superior does not have to personally take measures relevant to his duty to prevent or punish, and that he might, instead, delegate that responsibility of doing so to others. An example of this may be found in the Hadzihasanovic Appeals Judgement at paragraph 146 to 154, where reports of crimes committed at the Slavonija Furniture Salon were filed with the Bugojno district prosecutor, not by Mr. Hadzihasanovic himself, nor at his express direction, but by subordinates acting in the normal exercise of the obligation. The Appeals Chamber was satisfied in these circumstances that Mr. Hadzihasanovic could be said to have fulfilled his duty to punish. It is of relevance to note here, Your Honours, that the Appeals Chamber made that finding despite the fact that Mr. Hadzihasanovic had not seen the terms of the report, despite the absence of any -- any evidence of any investigation having been initiated by the judicial authorities to which it had been referred, and of any -- that any of the perpetrators was ever punished. Findings to the same effect were made by the Hadzihasanovic Trial Chamber in relation to crimes committed in Dusina which were not appealed by the Prosecution and they stand for a correct expression of international law on that point. This judicial pronouncement, Your Honours, also stand for the proposition that the superior is not required to act if and where he is satisfied that the matter has already been remedied to the competent authorities, or where those authorities have made it clear that they regard themselves as competent. Indeed, what customary international law criminalizes is not a failure to act per se, but the failure to act in the knowledge that such failure would constitute a gross dereliction of duty. Akin, in the words of the High Command case that our colleagues have cited from, to personal neglect amounting to a wanton, immoral disregard of the actions of his subordinates amounting to acquiescence. Any other interpretation of international law, the US Military Tribunal added, would go far beyond the basic principles of criminal law as known to civilised nations. This explained that under customary international law a superior does not have to get personally involved to fulfil his obligation if he knows that the authorities responsible to investigates and prosecute are competent and have been seized of the matter. In such a case, the superior would fulfil duty by standing aside. In the Ford v. Garcia case, the following jury instructions, which were entirely based on international law, were given, and I quote: "A commander may be relieved of the duty to investigate or to punish wrong-doers if a higher military or civilian authority establishes a mechanism to identify and punish the wrong-doers. In such a situation, the commander must simply do nothing to impede nor frustrate the investigation." And it goes on to say this: "A commander may fulfil his duty to investigate and punish wrong doers if he delegates this duty to a responsible subordinate. A commander has a right to assume that assignment entrusted to a responsible subordinate will be properly executed. On the other hand, the duty to investigate and punish will not be fulfilled if the commander knows, or reasonably should know, that the subordinate will not carry out his assignment in good faith, or if the commander impedes or frustrates the investigation." In its reply brief, the Prosecution has sought to undermine this precedent by suggesting that as a matter of American law, the Ford v. Garcia instructions do not carry the weight of a binding precedent. This might or might not be the case as a matter of American law, Your Honours, but it was certainly authoritative enough for the ICRC to take this precedent into account and to rely upon it in its customary law studies. It is really relevant to note that those instructions were based not on any interpretation of American law, as might have limited their relevance to American jurisdictions, but were intended to represent the general statement of general principles on this point. Not surprisingly, perhaps, these instructions were picked up by two of the most important --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. Judge Meron has a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Could you, in the course of your argument, Mr. Mettraux, enlighten us as to the differences in the responsibility of civilian versus military superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I shall arrive at this point, Your Honour, with certainty. Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Because when you speak of the absence of the authority, in the case of Mr. Boskoski to punish, is that what you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I shall reach that point when you reach the fact, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Excuse me, I didn't find the case you mention in the American courts in this binder. Can you give me a direction of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. It should be at page 28 of your binder, tab number 1. And I apologise if it wasn't clear enough. As I indicated Your Honour, these instructions in the Ford v. Garcia case were based solely on an expression of international law. And not surprisingly, perhaps, these instructions were picked by two of the most important records of US practice in international law. One, is the United States Practice in International Law, 1999-2001, Volume 1, by Sean Murphy, at page 308 to 309; and the American Journal of International Law, Volume 95, issue two, at page 394 and following. These instructions and the principle which they reflect, Your Honours, may perfect legal and practical sense, since the distribution of powers and competence within a given state or within a given chain of command would lose any meaning if it were otherwise. Think, for example, of the president of the United States, who constitutionally is the commander-in-chief of US armed forces. If, anywhere, crimes are believed to have been committed by US forces, the competent investigative and prosecuting authorities are required by law to seize themselves of the matter, investigate it, and, where appropriate, prosecute it. In most and possibly all cases, there will be no involvement of the president, despite the fact that he is the superior of those who committed the crimes and he might, in fact, never have been informed of the course of such proceedings. As a superior of those who committed the crimes, he is entitled to assume, as a matter of international law, that the competent organs are taking care of business unless he hears otherwise. The involvement in a criminal investigation of a superior that often will have no investigative competencies or skills and might in some cases wish to shield subordinates, might also intentionally or inadvertently result in unwarranted interferences with the course of the investigation. This judicial or quasi-judicial statement also stand for another principle, and that is that a superior may never have more than an expectation that subordinates will perform their duty legally and that perpetrators will be punished. But that expectation is recognised as sufficient by customary international law, unless there is evidence to rebut it. I have said earlier that our response was a qualified yes, and that is because customary international law set certain limits regarding the extent to which a superior may rely upon the acts of others and his own entitlement to assume that they are acting legally. This limitation was best articulated in the High Command case. When using the example again of the president of the United States, the Tribunal said this: "The President has the right to assume that details entrusted to responsible subordinates will be legally executed. The President of the United States is Commander-in-Chief of its military forces. Criminal acts committed by those forces cannot in themselves be charged to him on the theory of subordination. The same is true of other high commanders in the chain of command. Criminality does not attach to every individual in this chain of command from that fact alone. There must a personal dereliction. That can occur only where the act is directly traceable to him or where his failure to properly supervise his subordinates constitutes criminal negligence on his part. In the latter case, it must be a personal neglect amounting to a wanton, immoral disregard of the actions of his subordinates amounting to acquiescence. Any other interpretation of international law would go far beyond the basic principles of criminal law as known to civilised nations." This would be the case under customary international law, in our submissions, in two situations: One, the Strugar scenario, where a superior knows that the body to which he remits the case is part of a sham investigation. Two, the Ford v. Garcia hypothetical, where the superior has reason to know that the subordinate will not carry out his assignment in good faith, or if the commander impedes or frustrates the investigation. It is most significant in that regard, and this may answer Your Honour Judge Liu's question, that neither of these scenarios was proved and that the Trial Chamber instead specifically found, at paragraph 536 of the Judgement, without any appeal, that and I quote: "It is not shown that the failure of police to perform their duties is attributed to his order." That's Mr. Boskoski's order. And it goes on to say: "Or was known to Ljube Boskoski at the relevant time, or that it should have been anticipated by him." Aside from the two exceptions that I mentioned earlier, superior responsibility does not depend on proof having been made that an investigation was in fact triggered. Although in the Hadzihasanovic Trial Chamber Judgement the Trial Chamber rightly noted, paragraph 1062, that where one is shown to have been triggered, as in this case, it would show, and I quote: "That the accused did not fail in his duty to take the necessary and reasonable measures to punish the perpetrators." Subject to the two above mentioned exceptions, it is therefore sufficient for the purpose of customary international law that reporting to the competent authorities has occurred, that the superior is aware of it, and that he should have no reason to think that his subordinate will not carry out their assignment in good faith. It is not irrelevant to note in that context that Mr. Boskoski was actually thanked by the Office of the Prosecutor for the assistance that he and the organs of the ministry had given in this matter, and that at no point during the relevant period was there any suggestion that the competent organ of the ministries were failing in their duties. Instead the Office of the Prosecution expressed its satisfaction with the works performed by the Macedonian organs in this investigation. If more than the possibility of punishment was required as a matter of law, the liability of a superior would also be made dependant on the actions of people over whom the superior may have no control so that he could not advance the investigation further, nor increase the chance of punishment. In the present case, for instance, the Trial Chamber found, at paragraph 536, that Mr. Boskoski had no authority over the competent judicial authorities so that he could not in any way influence their choices and decision as regard the course of this investigation. In the present --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux, I see the main difference between your position and that of the Prosecution as this: The Prosecution says, as I understand it, that should there be a delegation by the commander, the commander, nonetheless, has a responsibility to carry out a further check to ensure that the due punishment has been -- has been carried out. You reject that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Not only do we reject this, we will establish the submissions of the Prosecution to be false and unsupported either in evidence or in law, and we will use the jurisprudence of this Chamber, in particular, in Hadzihasanovic and Blaskic, to establish the fact that contrary to the submissions of our colleague, there is no such requirement, whether that is a matter of customary international law and/or under the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. And if allowed to continue, Your Honour, I will reach that point in a moment. Your Honour, going back to Mr. Boskoski and his relation to the judicial ongoing investigation of those events as was going on in Macedonia at the time, it is worth mentioning that Mr. Boskoski had no right, no entitlement and, in fact, no access to the judicial file that contained the fruit of the judicial investigation. In this case, for instance, the Ministry of Interior did not even receive and had no right to receive the autopsy result that was conducted in Ljuboten, nor the result of the ballistic testing that was conducted, nor the result of the DNA samples of the victims. In those circumstances, Mr. Boskoski would have been unable to ascertain whether the chances of punishments were high or low, and whether the investigation may lead to the punishment of subordinates, or whether there was a higher likelihood of this. In such a case, it would be both wrong and unfair, in our submission, to expect and require a superior to do more vis-a-vis a process over which he has no control and to find him responsible for investigative failures that are attributable to others. More importantly, this is simply not the state of customary international law. It is perhaps no surprise that in 15 years, no Chamber of this Tribunal, no one Prosecutor of this Tribunal has ever put such a standard forward, and certainly not in the Boskoski case. This is, in our submission, should tell you something about the state of the law. Another danger that would result from a higher threshold is the risk and temptation of hindsight. Any determination pertaining to the triggering of an investigation has to be made, as the Trial Chamber correctly determined, based on the information at the disposal of the superior at the relevant time. And Mr. Boskoski was said by the Trial Chamber to have had no reason to doubt that the matter was, in fact, being properly handle by the judiciary. A higher standard of certainty would also have the affect of creating the sort of transfer of competence, from the judicial organs to the superior, which the ICRC warned against and which it said should not result from the doctrine of command responsibility. Commentary to Additional Protocol I, paragraph 3562. Instead, once the matter has been placed in the hands of competent organ, it is for them to investigate and decide how far it should go. Under customary international law, where a superior does not have personal powers to sanction, as in this case, the measure of whether that superior has fulfilled his duty to punish is therefore the contradiction that he or his subordinate have made to the triggering of an investigation by the competent organ, not the punishment of culpable subordinates, nor the likelihood that this will happen. As I just promised, Your Honour, we can establish each and all of these facts through the jurisprudence of this very Chamber. In Hadzihasanovic, for instance, the Appeals Chamber took the view that the mere fact that an incident was reported to investigative authorities by subordinate of Mr. Hadzihasanovic, was enough to satisfy his duty to punish, regardless of any consideration of a subsequent investigation by the competent organs, regardless of the chances or likelihood that Mr. Hadzihasanovic's effort might in fact lead to the punishment of the culprits, and regardless of the fact that there was no evidence that an investigation had, in fact, been initiated by the competent organs. And I refer to paragraph 147 and following of the Judgement. In the Blaskic case, Your Honour, the Appeals Chamber, at paragraph 418 to 420, found that the superior could be said to have fulfilled his duty to punish when a report was made to the competent authorities about a particular incident but in relation to which the superior received no further information and had, therefore, no way of ascertaining how likely the punishment was in this matter. Finding to the same effect may also be found in the Blaskic Appeals Chamber Judgement at paragraph 504, 505, and 507. Less authoritative perhaps, but no less relevant here, are the unappealed findings of the Hadzihasanovic Trial Chamber Judgement which made it clear that Hadzihasanovic could be said to have fulfilled his obligation to punish crimes in Dusina when subordinates reported the matter to the competent judicial authorities, although there was no indication that Hadzihasanovic knew of anything that happened thereafter, or whether an investigation was in fact conducted by the competent authorities. It is also important to note that despite the fact that the MOI had notified the competent judicial authorities, Mr. Boskoski continued to take active steps all through the relevant time with a view to attempt to ensure that organs of the MOI were assisting the ongoing judicial investigation, thereby going what was required of him under both domestic and international law. And I will come to that in a minute. We will discuss the document on under tab 13 that we have prepared for Your Honours. It will also be relevant that at the time when the Office of the Prosecution announced that they would exercise primacy over the Ljuboten case and when the case was eventually deferred to the jurisdiction of this Tribunal, the Macedonian judicial investigation was still ongoing and that the Prosecution suggested as one of the reasons for the deferral of the case, the risk that the Macedonian investigation and the OTP investigation might collide. There could therefore be no suggestion on the part of the Prosecution that this investigation, the Macedonian investigation, was unlikely to result in the punishment of the culprits, nor is there any finding in the Judgement to that effect. And to put, perhaps, in perspective the standard now put forth by the appellant, it might be worth noting that despite all its good will, and investigative might, this Prosecutor has made it no more than possible that any of the perpetrators of crimes at Ljuboten will ever be punished. Turning to the first and principle ground of appeal, Your Honours, and with the time left, I would simply ask you to turn to tab 3 of your binders, where you will find the text of paragraphs 406, 415, 417, 536, and the subheading at page 178 of the Judgement. The highlighted sections in this paragraph refer explicitly to the relevant legal standard of necessary and reasonable measures which the Prosecution claims the Trial Chamber failed to apply. Particularly important in that regard is paragraph 536 of the Judgement, one of those paragraphs ignored by the appellant brief which contain explicit finding to the effect that the Trial Chamber found, and I quote: "It is not shown that he," that is Mr. Boskoski, "failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures." This is the legal standard, Your Honours, which this appellant says the Trial Chamber should have applied and which it claims it failed to apply. And how does the Prosecution explain away the presence of finds that so plainly and unavoidably demonstrate that the Trial Chamber adopted the correct legal test? Well, in its appeal brief, the Prosecution said not a word of this particular finding, and not a word of most of the other relevant paragraph. This is a case, Your Honour, of an appellant that hangs on to the convenient findings of the Trial Chamber and is in denial on even on convenient ones. In paragraph 18 of its reply brief and after the appellant's blind ignorance of this paragraph had been exposed, the appellant simply declined to address this finding and claimed instead that paragraph 536, k and I quote: "Merely confirm the Chamber's use of the wrong legal test." While the unshakeability of the appellant commitment to his argument may be admired, its unwillingness to acknowledge its obvious lack of merit is to be deplored. Your Honours, the Judgement contains many clear and unassailable indications, and I have mentioned the relevant paragraph, and you can turn to tab 3, that the Trial Chamber in fact identified and applied the correct legal standard to come to the view that Mr. Boskoski had, in fact, adopted the necessary and reasonable measure in the circumstances. It may therefore be concluded that the Prosecution first and principle ground of appeal has no merit and should be rejected. Turning to the appellant's second and alternative ground of appeal. The Defence has already explained in its brief why the Prosecution should not be permitted to raise on appeal an issue that was not raised at trial, and I was content to hear our colleague, at page 65 and 66, agree that a party on appeal should not be permitted to do so. It might be worth reiterating that the Prosecution did not ask a single question of a single witness about either of the two documents, 1D6 and P46.16, that are the subject of this appeal. Nor did the Prosecution make a single reference to either of these documents in its final brief or final submission. And that is despite, Your Honour, extensive examination and cross-examination by the Defence in relation to these documents, and 40 or so references to them in its final brief. In its appellant brief, the Prosecution makes no attempt to explain its failure at trial to even acknowledge the existence and relevance of either of these documents. In its reply brief, with its failure having been exposed the appellant is telling that Rule 90(H)(ii) only required him to put the substance of the contrary of evidence to the witness and that this occurred at page 9249 to 9256 of the transcript. First, concerning the pages referred to by the appellant, the Appeals Chamber will have no difficulty ascertaining that the fact that neither of the documents, nor their content, is even hinted at by the Prosecution in these pages of the record, nor do these pages contain any suggestion on the part of the Prosecution that it was suggesting to the witness that Ministry of Interior reporting to the judiciary had been inadequate or that it would be insufficient for Mr. Boskoski to fulfil his duty to punish. Secondly, Rule 90(H)(ii) is not pertinent here not just because the Prosecution failure extended to both its witnesses and not just those that the Prosecution cross-examined, but also because it falls short of the standard of the Blaskic Appeals Chamber Judgement, at paragraph 222, which requires a party to raise before the Trial Chamber, and I quote: "Any issue that require resolution." Considering the extensive use of these two documents by the Defence in relation to the third element of command responsibility, the appellant could not possibly pretend to have been surprised by the reliance placed by the Trial Chamber on to these documents in relation to that very issue. Furthermore, when admitting P46, which is, Your Honour, a judicial file which contain, among others, P46.16, the Trial Chamber took notice of the Prosecution's submission that this file was said to be relevant to Mr. Boskoski's alleged failure to investigate and punish subordinates and admitted it on that basis. I refer Your Honours to the Trial Chamber decision of 14 May 2007, at paragraph 22. There was therefore no indication that the Prosecution could misunderstand or be oblivious to this fact that this document was to be regarded as relevant to this part of their case. Exhibit 1D6 was tendered and admitted on 15 May 2007 through Witness M-037, and I refer Your Honour to pages 848 to 857 of the transcript. This document was offered in evidence as relevant to the system of communication of information between the MOI, the Ministry of Interior, and the judicial organ as was relevant to establishing the MOI's contribution to the triggering and supporting of the judicial investigation into the events of Ljuboten. There was no objection on the part of the Prosecutor as regard either the admission of this document or its relevance to that part of the case. In light of this, no diligent counsel could have failed to make submissions as regards the relevance and weight of this document to this issue, without also being said to have waived his right to raise this issue for the first time on appeal. The second ground, Your Honour, should be rejected summarily on that basis. If however the Appeals Chamber wishes to consider the substance of the appeal on the second ground, I would draw Your Honours to the paragraph of 142 of the Hadzihasanovic Appeals Chamber Judgement, where Your Honours made it clear that the legal test relevant to the third element of command responsible is whether a reasonable trier of fact could conclude that the measure, or measures, adopted by a superior in particular circumstances can be regarded as necessary and reasonable in the circumstances. That statement of the law reflects and integrates the fact that under the doctrine of superior responsibility, a superior enjoys, and I quote: "Considerable latitude in the way in which he fulfilled his responsibilities." That quote, Your Honour, is from the authorative World War II Law Reports of the Trial of War Criminals, Volume 12, page 83 and 110. This means that under international law, a superior may not be held criminally responsible for choosing a particular course of action over another or for opting for a particular set of measures rather than others, unless that choice amounted to what is characterised under customary law as a gross dereliction of duty amounting, according to the High Command case, to acquiescence with the crimes. Applying that same logic, the High Command case made it clear, for instance, that the superior could not be held responsible for preferring disciplinary measures over criminal sanctions, or the other way around. If the measures which he chose appear to be adequate in the circumstances. At page 524 of the Judgement, the US Tribunal said this: "The duty imposed upon a military commander is the protection of the civilian population. Whether this protection be assured by the prosecution of soldiers charged with offences against the civilian population, or whether it be assured by disciplinary measures or otherwise, is immaterial from an international standpoint." This is why, for instance, in Blaskic, having been satisfied that the underlying incident in Ahmici which was relevant to the charges had been reported to the competent judicial authorities, the Appeals Chamber did not inquire further, nor seek to establish whether the accused could also have adopted disciplinary measures or conducted further investigation, nor did the Appeals Chamber suggest that he could be liable for failing to do so. This is also why the Appeals Chamber in Hadzihasanovic has said that the question of whether a superior has fulfilled his obligation is not resolved by the question of whether the measures were penal or disciplinary or a combination of both, but whether those that were adopted were appropriate in the circumstances. The same approach which was adopted by the Boskoski Trial Chamber is also consistent with Article 87(3) of Additional Protocol I. If the wish list approach advanced by the appellant in this case was accepted as law, it is not just the discretion of the superior that would be abolished and taken away, but so, too, would the significant margin of deference which Trial Chamber's possess when determining whether the measures adopted in a particular case were, in the circumstances, necessary and reasonable. I shall demonstrate in a few minutes how and why the Trial Chamber was well within its margin of appreciation when it took the view that Mr. Boskoski had, in fact, fulfilled his duties, and this can be established by asking and answering three questions. The first one is this: Under what circumstances does international law take the view that reporting to the competent authority suffice to fulfil a superior's duty to punish? Under international law we have already seen a superior may fulfil his obligation to punish by reporting the crimes to the competent authorities whenever he does not himself possess the power to punish or sanction. And I will come back in a minute when discussing Hadzihasanovic and Blaskic. In this case, the Prosecution never alleged and the Trial Chamber correctly found that, under Macedonian law, Mr. Boskoski had no power, nor any authority to punish or sanction the crime of murder, cruel treatment and wanton destructions that form the bases of the charges. The Trial Chamber was, therefore, correct in law and fact and well within its margin of appreciation when concluding that Mr. Boskoski could, in law, fulfil his duty to punish by having the matter reporting to the competent authority, as happened in this case, and as he was informed had happened. The second question that was to be addressed here is this: What effect, in law, does the reporting to the competent authorities have on a superior duty to punish? As we pointed out earlier, all statements of international law mentioned are unqualified where a superior cannot himself impose punishment, and once a superior or his subordinates have reported to the competent authority, the obligation of the superior to punish is displaced and the obligation is extinguished. This principle may be illustrated, contrary to what the Prosecution has suggested, with the statement of law of Judge Meron and Judge Kwon at paragraph 3 of their Strugar opinion where the two Judges, who were not dissenting on that point of law, rejected explicitly the Prosecution's submission that the superior would retain his duty to investigate, even where another person had been designated to carry out the investigation. And I draw your attention in particular to the footnote attached to that paragraph. This legal statement of principle is sound and may likewise be extracted from the Hadzihasanovic and Blaskic Appeals Chamber Judgements. As Your Honour will recall, in both of these cases, subordinates of the accused had sent reports to the competent investigative authorities. In both of these cases, the Appeals Chamber took the view that the accused had thereby fulfilled his obligation to punish in relation to crimes committed in the context of the incidents that were reported, and the Appeals Chamber did not conduct any further review of the record to establish whether the superior could have taken additional measures. The Appeals Chamber finding as to the effect of reporting in both of these cases was absolute, all encompassing and unqualified. And that is why also, as will be discussed in a moment, the Appeals Chamber never suggested that after reported had occurred, in the Blaskic case for instance, the Trial Chamber should further have satisfied itself whether the accused could have taken other measures such as disciplinary measures or further investigative steps, as the appellant now seeks to claim. In that sense, the Trial Chamber was entirely right and acting well within the boundaries of its discretion when taking the view that the matter, having been reported to the competent authorities, and in the absence of any suggestion that Mr. Boskoski was aware of any failure on the part of the MOI organ to perform the duties, he could be said to have fulfilled a duty to punish. The third and final question is this: What, in law, are the requirements for such reporting to have the effect of displacing the superior's duty to punish? According to the Prosecution, in order to fulfil his obligation to punish, Mr. Boskoski was required to report and I quote: "The allegation of criminal conduct by subordinates," it's in various parts of reply brief, "and should also have satisfied various other requirements of form." There is no legal or evidential support to back such a claim, and, in fact, it directly contradicts the jurisprudence of this very Chamber. Customary international law does not impose any requirement of form or content to the way, manner or shape of the reporting by a superior or his subordinates. Again, all legal statement, some of which you will find in tab 1 of our binder, are unqualified statements of law on that point. More interestingly and perhaps even more enlightening in that respect are the factual findings that have been made by this Chamber in the context of applying that standard and the principle that can be extracted from these. If you look, for instance, to paragraph 418 of the Blaskic Appeals Chamber Judgement, you will recall a finding of the Appeals Chamber to the effect that Blaskic had requested an investigation into the events of Amici and that the investigation was immediately taken over by SIS Mostar. Blaskic's instructions to his chief of security were, and I quote: "To carry out an investigation into the incident so that he could sends a report to Mostar." This was regarded as sufficient by the Appeals Chamber to displace his obligation to punish in relation to all crimes committed in Amici. And that despite the fact that -- the Appeals Chamber was aware that the investigation had been obstructed and conducted incompetently. No reference was made in that report pointing to subordinates as potential suspects, nor did the Appeals Chamber take the view that such a report should have listed crimes believed to have been committed during that incident. On that basis, at paragraph 420, and 422, the Appeals Chamber held that it was satisfied that Blaskic had fulfilled his obligation under Article 7(3) and should be acquitted of these crimes. Again similar finding and to the same effect may be found at paragraph 504, 507 and 511 of the Blaskic Appeals Chamber judgment. The Chamber would also be able to reach the same conclusion by reviewing its findings in the Hadzihasanovic case. At paragraph 146, this Chamber found that a subordinate of Mr. Hadzihasanovic had filed a report to the Bugojno municipal prosecutor regarding an incident that occurred on the 5th of August, 1993. The report did not refer to all the suspected crimes committed during that incident and in relation to which Mr. Hadzihasanovic was later charged for failure to punish, but the Appeals Chamber did not regard the incompleteness of the report as a basis to find that Hadzihasanovic had failed in his duty to report all of the crimes relevant to that incident, nor was the fact that there was no evidence that an investigation had actually been initiated by the local prosecutor, nor was the fact that the report failed to mention subordinates as potential suspects. What mattered for the purpose of Mr. Hadzihasanovic's responsibility under Article 7(3) is the fact that the incident in the context of which crimes were believed to have been committed was referred to the competent authorities so that the report created reasonable doubt as to whether his subordinate had initiated an investigation into relation to all crimes committed there. And contrary to what the appellant is now seeking to suggest, the Appeals Chamber explicitly found that the absence of a reference to some of the crimes believed to have been committed there, for instance, cruel treatment, did not undermine the reasonable doubt that the report had the effect of reporting what the Appeals Chamber characterised as the entire matter to the Bugojno prosecutor. Once reporting had occurred and as a matter of international law, Mr. Boskoski had therefore fulfilled his obligation. Under domestic Macedonian law, the responsibility to investigate and to expand the investigation where appropriate belonged to the judicial organs. As will be clear from our brief, and I don't need to repeat our submissions on that point at paragraph 213 and following, the judicial authorities were seized of the entire set of allegations which now form the basis of these charges. And after the report had been made to the competent authorities, Mr. Boskoski had no further obligation under customary international law as will have a reason only if and when he had received information that subordinates were interfering with the investigation, which the Trial Chamber found he never received. In those circumstances, and as the Trial Chamber found, Mr. Boskoski was acting in a manner consist with his obligation, and the Trial Chamber was well within the scope of its discretion. The appellant finally submits that should you find fault with the Trial Chamber's findings, you should reverse Mr. Boskoski's acquittal and convict him. The appellant made this extraordinary submission without saying a word in its appeal brief of how you, the Judges, could possibly reach that conclusion, and without saying a word of the evidence that would stand behind -- between the question of the decision and the relief which the appellant is seeking. This is therefore relief which, as we understand it, the Prosecutor is asking you to grant at face value and to ignore the evidence that is on the record. We prefer, however, Your Honour, to ask to you base your decision on the evidence in this case which is on the record, which we have identified in our brief, and which is described in detail in tab 13. There is no mention, for instance, in the appeal brief that on 13 August 2001, one day after events, and at his request, Mr. Boskoski met with the head of the OSCE to discuss the events of Ljuboten. That on the same day, and immediately after the meeting, he announced publicly that the truth about what happened should be established, and he immediately set up a commission of inquiry and appointed the three highest ranking officers of the ministry to head that commission, thereby by demonstrating his readiness and willingness to look into this incident and sending a powerful message to all organs of the ministry that they were expected to assist the judicial authorities in elucidating this matter. In its reply, the Prosecution suggests that the Chamber could not rely upon this measure, as the terms of reference of the commission were narrow and factually inaccurate because they referred to the MOI as having responded to a terrorist attack. This, however, was taken into account by the Trial Chamber which found, nevertheless, at paragraph 528, that the establishment of the commission, and I quote: "Indicates action which could be advanced as meeting his obligation pursuant to Article 7(3)." And whilst the terms of reference might with hindsight have proved to have been partly inaccurate, as the Trial Chamber noted, the Trial Chamber nowhere suggested that Mr. Boskoski was aware of these inaccuracies, and the evidence is clear that Mr. Boskoski was acting, as he was entitled to, upon the information which he has at his disposal at the time. More importantly, by ordering the review of these reports which he had received, he effectively sought to verify the accuracy of this report. The Prosecution also seek to dismiss Mr. Boskoski's public call of the same day, 13 August, that this matter should be fully investigated and should be elucidated whereby he put his political weight behind the investigative effort. The Prosecution suggest that you should disregard this because Mr. Boskoski expressed the belief that the victims had been terrorists not civilians. It is clear, however, Your Honours, from Exhibit 1D203, in combination with 1D24, among others, that Mr. Boskoski's view on that point was based on a good faith belief acquired from information that he this received both from the OSCE and from its ministry, that were consistent with the view that expressed. As explained earlier, the superior is entitled to trust and act upon information which he received from his chain of command unless he has reasonable to disbelieve it, and there is]was none here. And while the Prosecution seeks to discredit Mr. Boskoski's statement -- public statement, Exhibit P362 explicitly records Mr. Boskoski as saying this: "In order to discover the truth, the Prosecution will need authorisation to perform an exhumation in accordance with the legal procedure if we want the truth to be confirmed." Those, Your Honours, were not empty words, as a written recommendation was made on his behalf for an exhumation and autopsy which was sent to the competent judicial authorities, and upon which the judicial authorities acted. And according to the Mitevski report, that's Exhibit P378, such a measure was intended to achieve, and I quote: "Comprehensiveness and all-inclusiveness" with a view to "take necessary legal action towards confirmation of all relevant facts and receipt of an answer to the open substantive question about this event." And whilst the Trial Chamber found fault with the work of the commission, it took care to note, however, at paragraph 436, in fine, that its report -- that in its report, the commission did identify the need for exhumation of the buried as a step towards confirmation of the relevant facts and acknowledged that open substantive question of this event remained unanswered. Mr. Boskoski continued to take steps to push the issue of the Ljuboten investigation up the agenda all through the relevant period so as to make it clear to all those involved that they were expected to help elucidate this case. For instance, on 20 August and 4 September 2001 respectively, Mr. Boskoski reported the preliminary findings of his ministry to both the coordinative body of management of the crisis and the government. In reply, at paragraph 41, the Prosecution suggests that you should disregard this because Mr. Boskoski said in his report that victims were believed to have been terrorists. But again the Prosecution attributes to Mr. Boskoski power of hindsight, which unfortunately he does not possess. Mr. Boskoski was entitled to act based on the information that the competent organs of the ministry and the OSCE had provided him. It should be noted also furthermore that, at least as far as three of the victims were concerned, the Trial Chamber found that they could not conclude beyond a reasonable doubt that they had been civilians. It was also Mr. Boskoski who proposed and pushed for the drafting of a joint Ministry of Interior and Ministry of Defence joint report that, again, provided further impetus for the investigation and prevented the Ljuboten investigation from slipping away from the agenda. And it was he who provided more information to the government on 25th of September, 2001. Mr. Boskoski also publicly supported the idea that the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal should be involved in the investigation and provided that office with information, thereby displacing any suggestion that he was trying to shield anyone from punishment. And when he offered again, in early 2002, to assist with the exhumation process in Ljuboten, his assistance and that of the police was turned down by the Office of the Prosecutor who today claims that he should have done more in relation to this investigation. And all through the relevant period, Mr. Boskoski also put all relevant organs of the ministry at the disposal of the competent Macedonian judicial authorities and when they asked the Office of the Prosecutor, and during that time he did nothing that could be interpreted as an interference with the work of the competent investigative organs. And what's, Your Honours, of the hundred or so measures taken by the competent organs of the MOI with a view to elucidate these crimes? In the evidence-free world inhabited by the Prosecution, none of those are mentioned in its appeal brief, as if they were not relevant to the consideration of the Appeals Chamber which is asked to convict Mr. Boskoski for an alleged failure to punish. Ignore, therefore, if you are to believe the appellant, the fact that it is the MOI that notified the competent judicial organs that force had been used in the village and that the bodies lied in the streets of Ljuboten. Ignore that it is the reports of the MOI that triggered the judiciary into action. Ignore also that the competent organs of the ministry sought to obtain information from the villagers about what happened. Ignore that members of the MOI were part of the investigative team that was formed to enter Ljuboten after these events. Ignore that it is pursuant to an MOI recommendation that an exhumation autopsy was ordered by the judicial organs. Ignore that the ministry professional leadership sought to engage the international organisation present in Macedonia at that time to assist with the investigation. Ignore that the competent organs of the MOI responded to all judicial requests for assistance to the greatest extent feasible. Ignore that MOI organs took part in all preparatory meetings organised by the competent judicial organs and that they played a major part in the process of exhumation and autopsy. Ignore that it is they who conducted various technical and forensic examination that were relevant to this investigation. Ignore that the MOI provided information and support to the Office of the Prosecutor all through this time. Ignore that no one during that time complained of the work of the MOI, and ignore the fact that the MOI was thanked for its effort, including by the Office of the Prosecutor itself. Ignore also at paragraph 452 and following of the Judgement the Trial Chamber took notice of a number of relevant measures which, had it not found that the matter had been properly reported to the competent organs, it would have had to consider in that context.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Ignore also, Your Honour, the sensitive security situation in Macedonia at the time that prevented the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't ignore the interpreters request to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I will make amend, Your Honour, after the hearing with the interpreters who I am sure have suffered through my presentation, and I apologise do them. Ignore, Your Honour, the evidence that the security situation in the Republic of Macedonia at the time prevented the authorities from entering the village for many months. Ignore also that the lack of cooperation of the villagers denied the authorities access to eye-witness testimony from victims that could have helped identify the perpetrators. And ignore that the resources of the Macedonian state, and that of Ministry of Interior in particular, were being drained by the MOI's involvement into the fighting which the Trial Chamber said amounted to an armed conflict. Ignore, you are told in the reply brief, some of the steps taken by MOI because the result of those was used by the judiciary in relation to the investigation of crime against Albanian villagers but for the investigation of terrorist crimes committed by members of the NLA. So according to the appellant, the Ministry of Interior and the minister should be held criminally responsible because the judiciary, over which he had no control, chose to use the material for one purpose rather than another. Your Honour, the course that the Prosecution invites you to adopt is an unreasonable one that has no connection to the record of these proceedings and bears no relationship with the law of superior responsibility as recognised under customary international law. But because the Prosecution is never short of an argument, Your Honour, there is a new one, which has been put forward in the context of its appellant brief, which is to suggest that to the extent that some investigative steps might have been taken, this was an investigation to establish not the facts and circumstances relevant to this case but solely the identity of the seven dead persons. Before making that submission, has the appellant even looked at the autopsy reports and the evidence of its own witness, forensic doctor, Jakovski, who conducted some of those autopsies and which deal in detail not with the identity of the persons but with the causes and circumstances of their death. Has the appellant asked itself why if the matter pertained solely to the identity of the dead, the chief of the Mirkovci police, where abuses occurred, was interviewed by his colleague? Has the appellant taken any notice of the fact that the judicial investigation pertained not just to the events of the 12th of August but to the period 10 to 14, that covered each and all of the crimes charged in this case, not just the death of seven people. And I direct Your Honours to paragraph 213 to 230 of our brief. The appellant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Actually, I'm told you have one minute left.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I will simply, then, point to tab 4, 20 or 4, 19, I should say to tab 14, 24 and also to 14, 25 and tab 12, 9, and simply invite Your Honour to take notice of the fact that in each and every one of these documents, reference is being made, not to the identity of the victim, but to the cause, circumstances and other matter pertaining to these events. I will also note, Your Honour, that in its reply brief, the Prosecution seeks to assert that in his statement, Mr. Cakic indicated that he was only interested to identify the victims and nothing else. If that's the case, Your Honour, this was his responsibility. But we draw your attention to Exhibit P55.10, P55.11, P55.13 which was signed by Cakic himself, and which clearly referred to the cause, time and circumstances of their death. And, Your Honour, if I may correct one last matter before concluding, in its reply brief, the Prosecution refers to the so-called internal control, to take issue with the Defence submission that internal control could not act without complaint of a citizen or a victim. And it says that Mr. Ruseski, Kire Ruseski, does not suggest that at paragraph 6 of his statement, which is Exhibit P385. The Prosecution is correct. That statement, Your Honour, is to be found at paragraph 3 of Mr. Ruseski's statement. Your Honour, before I reiterate -- before I conclude, I will simply reiterate and adopt by reference the submissions that we've made in our respondent brief, and before giving the floor back to the Prosecution, I will expression our appreciation to Your Honours for their patience. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Judge Meron.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: I'm sure that you've answered my question regarding civilian versus military superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, I'm pretty sure, Your Honour, that I have not answered your question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Well, I think that, if you allow me to say so, when Judges ask a question, it is not quite correct to say, I will come to it. It is better practice to answer it right away. Being as it is, could you please explain to us how would the responsibilities of Mr. Boskoski vary had he been a military superior not a civilian minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, I apologise to start with, by not having answered your question earlier, Your Honour, and I should have done so at the time. The answer is multi-layered. I think the main issue relevant here is the absence of a chain of command similar to the sort of chain of command that you would find in a military context, where in fact the responsibility of guaranteeing the protection of the standards of humanitarian law is, as the Prosecution indicated, put very heavily on the shoulders of military leaders and commanders. In the context of a civilian leader, the distribution of that responsible is organised very differently. Whether it is in Macedonia or in any other country, the responsibility to prevent and punish is distributed differently between organs, depending on the constitutional and legal arrangement relevant here. And in the case of Macedonia, as with many civil law system, the responsibility to conduct criminal investigation is placed not upon the police but upon the judicial authorities which have the authority to use the assistance of the police in that context. In that sense, Your Honour, if you want the -- the making of the structure, relevant to the application of the doctrine of superior responsibility is very different.
