Furthermore, in the case of Mr. Boskoski, an important factor was the difference between the -- I would say the professional background of Mr. Boskoski, who is a lawyer by training and appointed as a political appointee to his position, there is a chain of command of professionals within the body which stops before the minister; whereas in the military context, each and all of the subordinates come, if you wish, from the same background and have the same responsibility. In that case, the responsibility is to conduct criminal investigation, and related issues belonged at no point and to no extent to the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: The Rome Statute would be sort of relevant to this argument, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour to the extent that it offers a different standard of mens rea, it certainly would. And it would also, as, Your Honour, I'm grateful for pointing that out, it specifically provides in the text of the Statute that where a subordinate does not have the ability to conduct an investigation himself that could lead to the punishment, he or she has, in fact, the ability to remit the matter to the competent authorities. So, yes, I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MERON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: To follow up Judge Meron's question, so is that your position that, in the jurisprudence of our Tribunal, there's no differences concerning with the mens rea of a military commander or a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: As I understand the jurisprudence of the Tribunal, Your Honour, there is, in fact, no distinction based per se on whether you are a civilian or a military leader. What is there, however, in the findings of this Tribunal, in this Appeals Chamber in particular, a mechanism at the disposal of military commanders which are not at the disposal of civilian superior that may be relevant to certain inferences that may be drawn in that regard, in particular the presence in the military context of a chain of command which has that very purpose. But Your Honour is quite correct to suggest that unlike the ICC system, there is no distinction in principle between the mens rea relevant to a civilian superior or to a military superior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: I think it's fair to say that the battle-lines are fairly drawn between the parties in this case, and, Your Honours, I'm not going repeat everything that I have already said. What I would like to touch upon are just three small matters. First of all, in relation to the case of Bemba. I think we've already -- we have already dealt with it now. That's dealing with a different statutory framework, and therefore may not be of direct relevance to an application in the proceedings here. So far as Hadzihasanovic and Blaskic are concerned, which my learned friend refers to at some length and relies upon to develop his notion of delegation and as some support for this notion, looking quickly, as I have been able to do, at the Blaskic Appeals Chamber Judgement on which he relies, it's curious that following on from paragraphs that he mentioned, the finding of the Appeals Chamber, having received additional evidence, was that the appellant lacked effective control over the military units responsible for the commission of crimes in the Ahmici area. So the final finding was not to as to whether or not he had in fact taken all the necessary and reasonable measures, although there is some discussion about it rightly, at paragraph 420, but it appears that wasn't really what they were dealing with. They were dealing with whether or not he actually had effective control over the subordinates. So it's perhaps moot as to how useful that case is, in -- to support his arguments. Secondly, in relation to Hadzihasanovic, again, the problem that perhaps all of us face in extracting anything useful from the Hadzihasanovic approach, is that on the particular facts of that case, the reason that he was acquitted was that the Appeals Chamber found that there was a reasonable doubt about whether any reports had been made. The issue, or one of the arguments that was made, as I understand it, by Hadzihasanovic was as to whether he had actually taken penal measures from that -- or one of the reasons why you found in the Hadzihasanovic Appeals Judgement the determination that it doesn't really matter what you call them, whether they're disciplinary measures or criminal measures. One doesn't want to get bogged down, as it were, in precisely what the term is that you apply to the type of the measure. Hadzihasanovic, however, was aware that there had been an investigation, that perpetrators had been identified, that crimes had been identified, that some form of punishment, at least 60 days imprisonment had been imposed upon them, and he, therefore, said, Well, as I understood it, they'd been punished. All the measures that needed to be taken had been taken. Appeals Chamber took the view that in fact the measures were disciplinary measures and, therefore, there was more that needed to be done, but then went on to find that there was a reasonable doubt about whether actually a report had gone on to the public prosecutor, and, therefore, the accused should benefit from that reasonable doubt - quite rightly - and he was acquitted. So I'm not sure it's as helpful to my learned friend as he thinks it is. Your Honours, as I've said, the battle-lines are fairly drawn. We have addressed at length between us over the course of this afternoon the issues between the parties, and I don't propose so say any more at this stage, other than to deal with the binder that has been handed up to Your Honours. I only saw it just before you came back into court, and so I didn't have an opportunity to look through it to see whether there was any material in it that perhaps ought not to be placed before Your Honours. We do have some concerns over tab 13, where the analysis has been made, and it would appear to be an impermissible filing, or an additional impermissible filing, because there is a commentary at the side of the measures taken by competent MOI organs, and that isn't strictly what should be done. That's -- would count against the word limits and the filings before the Court, and there is no permission to file any additional material that comments or analyses what's gone on. So, Your Honours, I think that should be removed from the bundle, because it's not transcript, it's not pieces of evidence, and it's not Trial Judgement or other case references. It's an analysis by the respondent as to what he says the various documents amount to, and that's not, in our submission, permissible. So we would ask that that part of the brief be removed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux, let me hear you on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. Simply to explain what that document is, Your Honour. It is simply a support used, for our purposes, to direct Your Honours to the various measures that we've indicated during our submissions. This document is nothing other than a chronological reordering of the measures which have listed in our brief. There is nothing new in terms of submissions, in terms of references to what has already been said in our brief, Your Honour. It was done for the purpose of assisting the Chamber in having a snap-shot, if you want, of the chronological order in which measures were taken by both Mr. Boskoski personally and by the various organs of the Ministry of Interior, as were explained in a different fashion in our case. There is nothing new. There can be no suggestion of any prejudice or anything new coming out of this document that the Prosecutor could point to. It was simply a hope, one, to accelerate matters in the presentation; and to provide Your Honours with some degree of assistance, in terms of chronological mapping of the measures that were taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would it help, Mr. Rogers, if you could read into it as prepared by counsel. It is really just to assist. It's an aid, as far as can I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROGERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the difficulty is, is that we all labour under the Rules that are imposed upon us, and to come to court to the hearing and to try to impermissibly file a matter which adds argument, effectively, is not right. It's not something that the Prosecution would be permitted to do, and it's not something that the defendant -- the respondent should be permitted to do. If he had wanted to organise his materials better, he should have done it in his brief. I understand Your Honour's point, that it is an attempt to try to be helpful; but the help should have been provided within the brief and not in this way. Those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux, we'll disregard it. What remains now is to ascertain from Mr. Tarculovski whether he wishes to avail himself of the opportunity to make a personal statement. If you wish to do that, Mr. Tarculovski, you may do so, but for no more than 15 minutes. MR. A. DERSHOWITZ: He does wish to, yes. Thank you. THE ACCUSED TARCULOVSKI: [Interpretation] Your Honours, first of all, I'd like to point out that I really regret the loss of life. I myself have a family, and I sympathise with their deep pain. Personally I would never hurt innocent people. The President sent me to be in the region in order to coordinate and to report to him about the events throughout this action, if there's problem between -- to report if there is problems between the army and police. I did not organise anyone to do any harm. I'm sorry for the suffering experienced by both sides, and I'm hopeful there will be permanent peace in Macedonia between all sides. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tarculovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit -- you may sit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Boskoski, I'm to ask you whether you wish to make a statement. Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We have discussed the matter with Mr. Boskoski prior to the hearing, and he has indicated that there is no need for him to address the Court, but he is grateful for the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, in that case, we'll be -- we'll adjourn, and I wish to thank all the parties for the submissions which they have made and which the Trial Chamber has found helpful.
